title: German at Home
pronunciation_guide: English-friendly respelling for standard German, built from tools/de-lexicon.json (one entry per word). CAPITALS mark the stressed syllable.

phrases.note: Steh auf! comes from aufstehen (to get up). In a command the auf splits off and jumps to the end.
Zeit zum Aufstehen = time for getting up. Aufstehen has a capital A here because it's used as a noun.
Raus = out. After aus, das Bett changes to dem Bett – aus always triggers this 'dem' form.

phrases.de: Raus aus dem Bett, und zwar sofort!
phrases.ph: rows ows daym bet, unt tsvahr zo-FORT
phrases.note: Und zwar sofort = and I mean right now. Und zwar adds weight, like 'and what's more'.
Komm schon = come on (literally 'come already'). Very common for hurrying or encouraging someone.
Zu spät kommen = to be late, literally 'to come too late'. German uses the present tense for the near future.
Spät dran sein = to be running late. Schon means already – it's one of the most useful little words in German.
Wach = awake. To make a yes/no question, just put the verb first: Du bist wach → Bist du wach?
Past tense pattern: hast … geschlafen. The helper verb comes second and the ge- word goes to the very end.

phrases.en: What time did you go to sleep?
phrases.note: Schlafen gehen = to go to bed. Verbs of movement like gehen use sein in the past: bist … gegangen, not hast.
Duschen = to shower, and die Dusche = the shower. The past form just adds ge- and -t: geduscht.
Gehen + another verb needs no 'zu': Geh duschen! = Go and shower. Same with Geh schlafen! (Go to sleep!)
Anziehen = to put on / dress. Dich means 'yourself', and the an splits off and goes to the end.
Angezogen = dressed. It comes from anziehen, and the ge- squeezes in after the an: an-ge-zogen.

phrases.de: Hast du dir die Zähne geputzt?
phrases.ph: hast doo deer dee TSAY-nuh ge-PUTST
phrases.note: Germans 'clean themselves the teeth': dir = for yourself. Die Zähne is the plural of der Zahn (tooth).

phrases.de: Hast du dir die Haare gemacht?
phrases.ph: hast doo deer dee HAH-ruh ge-MAKHT
phrases.note: Die Haare = hair, but plural – Germans usually talk about hair as lots of hairs. Sich die Haare machen = to do your hair.
Alles = everything. It's not a noun, so it stays lowercase. Alles klar? = All good?
Der Schuh = shoe, die Schuhe = shoes. Wo means where – don't mix it up with wer (who).
Die Jacke is the everyday word for a coat or jacket. Der Mantel is a longer, smarter coat.
Der Rucksack becomes deinen Rucksack because it's the thing being forgotten. Nicht goes right at the end.
Das Pausenbrot = the sandwich you eat at break (Pause + Brot). German pupils usually take a snack, not a big lunch.
Das Handy = mobile phone. It looks English, but English speakers never call a phone that – it's a German invention.
Der Schlüssel = key, and the plural is also Schlüssel. Deine (not dein) tells you it means keys here.

phrases.en: What time do you need to leave?
phrases.note: Los on its own means 'off'. Germans often skip the verb: Ich muss los = I've got to go.

phrases.en: What time do you need to be there?
phrases.note: Da = there. With musst, the second verb (sein) is pushed to the end of the sentence.
Fertig means both 'ready' and 'finished', so this can also mean 'Are you done?'
Bald = soon. Bist du bald fertig? is literally 'Are you soon ready?' – a gentle hurry-up.
Los! = Go! / Come on! Adding jetzt (now) makes it more impatient.
From sich beeilen (to hurry). The dich = yourself, so it's literally 'hurry yourself!'
Short for losgehen or losfahren. Wir müssen los is the standard way to say 'we need to go'.
Warten auf = to wait for. Always use auf, never für: Ich warte auf dich, not für dich.
Alle = everyone (literally 'all'). Unlike English 'everyone is', it takes a plural verb: alle warten.

phrases.de: Wir fahren in fünf Minuten los.
phrases.ph: veer FAH-ren in fewnf mi-NOO-ten lohs
phrases.note: Losfahren = to set off (by car). The los splits off and goes to the end. On foot you'd say losgehen.
Gehen here means 'leave', not just 'walk'. Ich gehe jetzt = I'm off now.
Einsteigen = to get in (a car, bus, train). Ins is short for in das. Or just say: Steig ein!
Der Morgen (capital M) = the morning. Careful: morgen with a small m means tomorrow.
Der Wecker = alarm clock, from wecken (to wake someone). Klingeln = to ring.
Der Wecker changes to deinen Wecker because it's the thing being heard. Gehört comes from hören (to hear).
Einschlafen = to fall asleep. The ein splits off to the end; wieder = again.
Das Bad is short for das Badezimmer (bathroom). Frei = free or available.
German has a verb for eating breakfast: frühstücken. The noun is das Frühstück.

phrases.en: Have some breakfast before you go.
phrases.note: After bevor (before) the verb goes to the end: bevor du gehst. Was here is short for etwas (something).
Anziehen again: the an goes to the end. Same verb for any clothes: Zieh deine Jacke an!
Dir die Jacke = 'the jacket on yourself'. Germans often say die (the) where English says your.
Sauber = clean. Die Schuluniform exists, but most schools in Germany don't have a uniform at all.
Noch = still / more. Noch fünf Minuten = five more minutes. Die Minute, plural Minuten.
From weggehen (to go away). Blunt – fine to a sibling, rude to almost anyone else.
Raus! = Out! Short, sharp and rude-ish. It's short for heraus.
Das Zimmer = room. After aus, mein changes to meinem.
Müde = tired. Don't confuse it with mude – the dots on ü change the sound, so always write them.
Todmüde = dead tired (tod = dead + müde = tired). German loves sticking words together like this.
Auf sein = to be up (out of bed). The little word ja adds 'I already told you!'
Ich steh is a relaxed way of saying ich stehe. Ja schon = 'alright, I'm already doing it!'
Aufhören = to stop. Hör auf zu … = stop doing …: Hör auf zu nerven! (Stop annoying me!)
Germans say 'I don't find' rather than 'I can't find'. Nicht goes to the end here.
Die Haarbürste = Haar (hair) + Bürste (brush). A joined-up word takes the gender of its last part: die Bürste.
In Ruhe lassen = to leave in peace. Die Ruhe = peace and quiet.
Früh = early, spät = late. Viel zu = far too, so viel zu früh = way too early.
Germans 'have no hunger': Hunger haben = to be hungry. Hab is a chatty short form of habe.
Ja schon adds impatience: 'I'm coming, alright!' Komm is a casual short form of komme.
Ausmachen = to switch off. The aus jumps to the end. The opposite is anmachen (switch on).
Zuziehen = to pull shut. Der Vorhang = curtain, plural die Vorhänge.
Überhaupt nicht = not at all. Handy for moaning: Das ist überhaupt nicht fair!

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.de: Ich will nicht in die Schule.
phrases.ph: ish vil nisht in dee SHOO-luh
phrases.note: False friend: ich will = I want, not I will. Germans often drop gehen after wollen.
Sich fühlen = to feel. The mich (myself) is needed: literally 'I feel myself not well'.
Jemand = someone. Im is short for in dem: im Bad = in the bathroom.

phrases.en: He's been in there for ages!
phrases.de: Er ist schon ewig da drin!
phrases.ph: ayr ist shohn AY-vish dah drin
phrases.note: Ewig = forever. German uses the present tense with schon where English says 'has been'. For a sister: Sie ist …

phrases.en: Who used all the hot water?
phrases.de: Wer hat das ganze warme Wasser verbraucht?
phrases.ph: vayr hat das GAN-tsuh VAR-muh VA-ser fer-BROWKHT
phrases.note: Verbrauchen = to use up. Germans say warmes Wasser for hot water from the tap; heiß sounds scalding.

phrases.en: Can you take me in the car?
phrases.note: Kannst du …? = Can you …? Fahren here means 'drive someone somewhere', so no word for car is needed.
Schon wieder = yet again – great for complaining. Boah is a teen-style groan. Days are all der: der Montag.
Beeil dich = hurry up (sich beeilen). Im Bad = in the bathroom; im is short for in dem.

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.note: Brauchen = to need. Literally 'How long do you still need?' – the normal way to ask this.
Andere = other people. After müssen, Germans often drop the verb gehen: ins Bad müssen = need the bathroom.

phrases.de: So gehst du nicht aus dem Haus!
phrases.ph: zoh gayst doo nisht ows daym hows
phrases.note: So = like that. Das Haus becomes dem Haus after aus. A classic strict-parent line.
Aussehen = to look (appearance). The aus splits off and goes to the end: Du siehst … aus.
Sauber = clean; the opposite is schmutzig (dirty) or, more casually, dreckig.
Der Föhn = hairdryer (also the name of a warm Alpine wind). It becomes den Föhn because it's being switched off.
Leise = quiet, leiser = quieter. Add -er to compare, just like English: laut → lauter (louder).

phrases.en: You've been in there for ages.
phrases.de: Du bist ja schon seit Stunden da drin.
phrases.ph: doo bist yah shohn zite SHTUN-den dah drin
phrases.note: Seit = since/for. German uses seit with the present tense: du bist seit Stunden = you've been for hours.
Aufmachen = to open. The auf goes to the end. Die Tür = the door.

phrases.en: Put a jumper on, it's cold.
phrases.de: Zieh einen Pulli an, es ist kalt.
phrases.ph: tsee EYE-nen PU-lee an, es ist kalt
phrases.note: Der Pulli is short for der Pullover (jumper). Es ist kalt = it's cold; mir ist kalt = I'm cold.

phrases.de: Der Rock ist viel zu kurz.
phrases.ph: dayr rok ist feel tsoo kurts
phrases.note: Der Rock = skirt – a false friend, nothing to do with rock music. Zu kurz = too short.
Zu viel = too much (two separate words). Das Make-up is borrowed straight from English.

phrases.en: Don't leave your towel on the floor.
phrases.de: Lass dein Handtuch nicht auf dem Boden liegen!
phrases.ph: las dine HANT-tookh nisht owf daym BOH-den LEE-gen
phrases.note: Liegen lassen = to leave lying around. Das Handtuch (hand + cloth) is the word for any towel.
Das Oberteil = top (literally 'upper part'). Etwa adds suspicion, like 'Is that my top, by any chance?'

phrases.en: Your clothes are on the chair.
phrases.de: Deine Sachen liegen auf dem Stuhl.
phrases.ph: DYE-nuh ZA-khen LEE-gen owf daym shtool
phrases.note: Die Sachen = things, often used for clothes. Germans say clothes 'lie' (liegen) on a chair.

phrases.en: It's still in the washing machine.
phrases.de: Das ist noch in der Waschmaschine.
phrases.ph: das ist nokh in dayr VASH-ma-shee-nuh
phrases.note: Noch = still. Die Waschmaschine takes die from its last part, die Maschine.
Was anderes = something else (short for etwas anderes). Anderes gets a small a here.
Länger = longer, from lang. Nicht länger = not any longer.

phrases.de: Passt schon, du siehst super aus!
phrases.ph: past shohn, doo zeest ZOO-per ows
phrases.note: Passt schon = it's fine / that'll do – very common. Super is used just like in English.
German has no -ing form. Gerade (right now) shows you're in the middle of it.
Ich dusche can mean 'I shower' or 'I'm showering' – German uses one present tense for both.
Germans are 'under' the shower, not in it: unter der Dusche.

phrases.de: Ich mache mir gerade die Haare.
phrases.ph: ish MA-khuh meer ge-RAH-duh dee HAH-ruh
phrases.note: Sich die Haare machen = to do your hair. Mir = for myself, and die Haare is plural.
Sich schminken = to put make-up on. Die Schminke is make-up; das Make-up is used too.

phrases.de: Ich putze mir gerade die Zähne.
phrases.ph: ish PUT-suh meer ge-RAH-duh dee TSAY-nuh
phrases.note: Putzen = to clean. The same verb is used for cleaning the house: Ich putze das Bad.
False friend: fast means almost, not quick. Quick is schnell.

phrases.en: I'll be ready in five minutes.
phrases.de: In fünf Minuten bin ich fertig.
phrases.ph: in fewnf mi-NOO-ten bin ish FER-tish
phrases.note: Verb second: when a time phrase comes first, the verb (bin) comes next and ich moves after it.
Der Moment = moment. Moment! or Moment mal! is the everyday way to say 'hang on'.
Gib is the command form of geben (to give). Mir = me, as in 'to me'.
Warte = wait. Adding mal softens a command and makes it sound more natural.
Kommen = to come. Germans say ich komme even when English says 'I'm coming' – no -ing needed.

phrases.en: I'll be there in a minute.
phrases.note: Gleich = in a moment. It also means 'same', so watch the context. Da = there.
Runter = down, short for herunter. Ich komme runter = I'm coming down.
Die Klamotten = clothes (casual, like 'gear'). It's always plural, so it's sind, not ist.
Der Hoodie is used in German too. The 'proper' word is der Kapuzenpulli (hood + jumper).
Die Jeans works as one or several pairs. Gesehen comes from sehen (to see).
Meine (not mein) because Schuhe is plural. Sind (are) also matches the plural.
Das hier = this one here. Adding hier makes it clear which thing you're pointing at.
Trocken = dry; nass = wet. The washing is either trocken or noch nass (still wet).
Waschen = to wash. Watch the vowel change: ich wasche, but du wäschst and er wäscht.
Starting with das for emphasis is fine – the verb (brauche) still comes second. Morgen = tomorrow.
Geh raus = go out. Slightly less snappy than just Raus! but still firm.
Zumachen = to close. The zu goes to the end. Opposite: Mach die Tür auf!
Using the plain verb (reinkommen) as a command is short and bossy, like on a sign. Rein = in.
Sich umziehen = to get changed. Careful: umziehen without mich means to move house.
Besetzt = occupied or engaged – also what you hear when a phone line is busy.

phrases.en: Are you going to be long in the bathroom?
phrases.de: Brauchst du noch lange im Bad?
phrases.ph: browkhst doo nokh LANG-uh im baht
phrases.note: Noch lange = much longer. Literally 'Do you still need long in the bathroom?'
Es gibt = there is / there are. One of the most useful phrases in German.
Der Föhn = hairdryer. The ö is important – without it the word doesn't exist.
Alle sein = to be all gone (chatty). Alle normally means 'all' or 'everyone'.

phrases.de: Es ist kein Klopapier mehr da.
phrases.ph: es ist kine KLOH-pa-peer mayr dah
phrases.note: Das Klo = the loo, so das Klopapier = loo roll. Kein … mehr = no more …

phrases.en: Does this look OK on me?
phrases.note: Stehen normally means to stand, but jemandem stehen means to suit someone. Mir = me.
Zum Anziehen = to wear. Anziehen gets a capital A because zum turns it into a noun.
Das Frühstück = breakfast. Fertig means ready here – Essen ist fertig! = Food's ready!
Das Mittagessen = lunch (Mittag = midday + Essen = meal). Abendessen is dinner.
fertig means ready, and also finished. Das Abendessen (evening meal) is a das word, so it's always das Abendessen.
essen (to eat) becomes das Essen (food, meal) when used as a noun, and nouns always get a capital letter.
Komm essen! is literally 'come eat'. German skips the 'and': komm + another verb, e.g. Komm spielen! (Come and play!).
hol comes from holen (to fetch). hol dir = get yourself, so this is 'come, fetch yourself your dinner'.

phrases.en: What do you want for breakfast?
phrases.note: zum is short for zu dem. Use it for meals: zum Frühstück (for breakfast), zum Mittagessen, zum Abendessen.

phrases.en: What do you want for lunch?
phrases.note: das Mittagessen = lunch (Mittag = midday). In many German families this is the main hot meal of the day.
Germans 'have' hunger: Hast du Hunger? = Do you have hunger? Hunger is a noun, hence the capital H.

phrases.en: Do you want something to eat?
phrases.note: möchtest = would like. After möchtest, the second verb (essen) goes right to the end of the sentence.
In speech, was here is short for etwas (something), not 'what'. So: 'would you like something to drink?'

phrases.en: What do you want to drink?
phrases.note: willst is from wollen (to want). Careful: ich will means 'I want', not 'I will'.
German usually has no word for 'some' here: Möchtest du Wasser? is just 'would you like water?'
noch means 'still' or 'more of the same'. Möchtest du noch was? = Would you like some more (of it)?
reichen = to be enough. Reicht das? is short and very common. Answer: Ja, das reicht! (Yes, that's enough!)
aufessen = to eat up. In the past form the ge slips into the middle: auf-ge-gessen.
Iss! is the du-command of essen: the e changes to i (essen → du isst → Iss!). Double s, no t.
wenigstens = at least. Probier! is the command from probieren (to try, especially food).
doch softens a command, like 'go on'. ein bisschen = a little bit, a phrase you'll use constantly.

phrases.de: Du hast es noch nicht mal probiert!
phrases.ph: doo hast es nokh nisht mahl pro-BEERT
phrases.note: noch nicht mal = not even. Handy for complaints: Du hast noch nicht mal gefragt! (You didn't even ask!)
German has no word for 'don't' in commands. Just give the command and add nicht: Iss das nicht! = Don't eat that!
gleich here means 'in a moment'. It can also mean 'the same', so listen for context.

phrases.en: It'll be ready in ten minutes.
phrases.de: Es ist in zehn Minuten fertig.
phrases.ph: es ist in tsayn mi-NOO-ten FER-tish
phrases.note: German often uses the present tense for the future when a time is given: Es ist in zehn Minuten fertig = it is ready in ten minutes.

phrases.en: Put your plate in the dishwasher.
phrases.de: Stell deinen Teller in die Spülmaschine!
phrases.ph: shtel DYE-nen TE-ler in dee SHPEWL-ma-shee-nuh
phrases.note: der Teller (plate) becomes deinen Teller because it's the thing being moved. die Spülmaschine = dishwasher.
Wirf! comes from werfen (to throw), so it's 'throw that in the rubbish'. der Müll = rubbish.

phrases.en: Put it back in the fridge.
phrases.de: Stell es wieder in den Kühlschrank!
phrases.ph: shtel es VEE-der in dayn KEWL-shrank
phrases.note: der Kühlschrank = fridge, literally 'cool cupboard' (kühl = cool, Schrank = cupboard). wieder here means 'back'.
den Tisch decken = to set the table (decken = to cover). Kannst du ...? = Can you ...? with the verb at the end.
abräumen = to clear away. After kannst du it stays in one piece at the end; as a command it splits: Räum ab!
ausräumen = to unload (aus = out). Its partner einräumen means to load. Same verb, just swap aus/ein.
einräumen = to put things in (ein = in). Germans also say einräumen for putting away shopping.

phrases.de: Wer hat das hier liegen lassen?
phrases.ph: vayr hat das heer LEE-gen LA-sen
phrases.note: liegen lassen = to leave lying around. Careful: wer means 'who', not 'where' (that's wo).

phrases.de: Wer hat das letzte Stück gegessen?
phrases.ph: vayr hat das LETS-tuh shtewk ge-GE-sen
phrases.note: das Stück = piece. Super useful for cake, pizza or chocolate: ein Stück Kuchen = a piece of cake.
Lass! comes from lassen (to leave, to let). Lass das! on its own is also a common way to say 'Stop that!'

phrases.en: Wash your hands before you eat.
phrases.de: Wasch dir vor dem Essen die Hände!
phrases.ph: vash deer fohr daym E-sen dee HEN-duh
phrases.note: Germans say 'wash to yourself the hands': dir die Hände, not deine Hände. vor dem Essen = before the meal.
sich hinsetzen = to sit down. dich means 'yourself', and the hin jumps to the end of the command.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.de: Gibst du mir mal das Salz?
phrases.ph: geepst doo meer mahl das zalts
phrases.note: Gibst du mir ...? is literally 'Do you give me ...?' Germans often ask for things this way, and mal makes it sound casual.
heiß (hot) is spelt with ß, which sounds like ss. Vorsicht! = Careful! and is also what warning signs say.
Guten Appetit! is said just before everyone starts eating. The usual reply is Danke, gleichfalls! (Thanks, you too!)

phrases.en: Don't eat with your mouth open.
phrases.note: After mit, adjectives change their ending: offen (open) becomes offenem. der Mund = mouth.
das Handy is the German word for mobile phone. It looks English, but English speakers never use it that way.
Ist noch ... da? = Is there still ... there? This is the everyday way to ask if any of something is left.

phrases.de: Kannst du mir beim Kochen helfen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer bime KO-khen HEL-fen
phrases.note: helfen always takes mir (not mich): Hilf mir! = Help me! beim Kochen = with the cooking.
schmecken = to taste (good). For food, Germans ask 'did it taste good to you?' rather than 'did you like it?'
gibt's is short for gibt es (there is). Was gibt's? = What is there? and also means 'What's up?'
wann = when (in questions). Careful: wenn also means 'when', but not in questions.
schon = already or yet. Adding it makes the question sound a bit impatient, which suits a hungry teenager.
Question word first, then the verb second: Was essen wir? Word for word 'What eat we today?'
hab is the spoken short form of habe. Germans 'have' hunger, just like Hast du Hunger?
verhungern = to starve to death, so it's just as dramatic as the English. Also common: Ich hab einen Riesenhunger (giant hunger).
Gibt es ...? = Is there ...? was zu essen = something to eat; zu + verb works like English 'to'.

phrases.en: Can I have something to eat?
phrases.de: Kann ich was zu essen haben?
phrases.ph: kan ish vas tsoo E-sen HAH-ben
phrases.note: Kann ich ... haben? = Can I have ...? The haben goes to the very end. Swap in anything: Kann ich Geld haben?

phrases.de: Darf ich mir einen Snack nehmen?
phrases.ph: darf ish meer EYE-nen snek NAY-men
phrases.note: Darf ich ...? = Am I allowed to ...? It's more polite than kann ich. der Snack is borrowed from English.
noch mehr = even more / some more. noch adds the idea of 'on top of what I've had'.
mir = for me / to me. Kannst du mir ... machen? = Can you make me ...? e.g. Kannst du mir einen Toast machen?
können (can) becomes können with wir: ich kann, du kannst, wir können. The main verb (essen) goes to the end.
German has no single word for takeaway; people say Essen bestellen (order food). bestellen = to order.
Use zu when going to a shop or restaurant by name: zu McDonald's, zu Lidl. gehen goes to the end.
mag is from mögen (to like). Das goes first for emphasis, so ich comes after the verb: the verb always stays in second place.
will = want, not 'will'. It's a classic false friend: Ich will Pizza means 'I want pizza'.
With a noun, German uses kein (no) instead of nicht: keinen Hunger = no hunger.
gegessen is the past form of essen. hab goes second and gegessen goes right to the end. schon = already.
German happily uses the present for the future when there's a time word: Ich esse später = I'm eating later.

phrases.en: Can I eat in my room?
phrases.de: Kann ich in meinem Zimmer essen?
phrases.ph: kan ish in MY-nem TSI-mer E-sen
phrases.note: das Zimmer = room. After in (meaning 'where something is'), mein becomes meinem.
das Knabberzeug = nibbly stuff (knabbern = to nibble, Zeug = stuff). It covers crisps, nuts and pretzels.
False friend: Chips in German are crisps. If you want chips (fries), ask for Pommes.
noch here means 'still': Haben wir noch ...? = Have we still got ...? die Schokolade is a die word.

phrases.de: Wer hat mir mein Essen weggegessen?
phrases.ph: vayr hat meer mine E-sen VEK-ge-ge-sen
phrases.note: weggegessen = ate (so it's gone). weg means away. mir adds 'on me', like 'who ate my food on me?'
aufheben = to save for later. Watch out: it also means to pick up, as in Heb das auf! (Pick that up!)
Darf ich ...? = May I ...? It's the polite way to ask permission; parents usually like it better than kann ich.

phrases.en: Can you get me some water?
phrases.note: holen = to go and get, to fetch. Kannst du mir ... holen? = Can you get me ...?
lecker = tasty, the everyday word for good food. echt = really, very common in teen speech.
satt = full (of food). Don't say Ich bin voll: that means 'I'm drunk'!

phrases.en: Can you pass me the salt?
phrases.de: Kannst du mir bitte das Salz reichen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer BI-tuh das zalts RY-shen
phrases.note: reichen here means to pass or hand over. It's the same verb as in Reicht das? (Is that enough?)

phrases.de: Es ist keine Milch mehr da.
phrases.ph: es ist KYE-nuh milsh mayr dah
phrases.note: kein ... mehr = no more. keine Milch mehr = no more milk. Same pattern: Ich habe keine Zeit mehr.
mir = for myself. der Toast is borrowed from English, and Toastbrot is the sliced bread you use.
zu before an adjective means 'too': zu heiß (too hot), zu kalt (too cold), zu scharf (too spicy).

phrases.de: Soll ich dir beim Kochen helfen?
phrases.ph: zol ish deer bime KO-khen HEL-fen
phrases.note: Soll ich ...? = Shall I ...? It's how you offer to do something. dir = you, because helfen takes dir, not dich.
war is the past of ist (was). Teens stick super- in front of adjectives: superlecker, supernett.
ordentlich = properly, neatly. It slots in before hin, which still jumps to the end of the command.
vom is short for von dem (off the / from the). der Ellbogen stays the same in the plural: die Ellbogen.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.note: Sprich! is the command of sprechen (to speak): the e changes to i, like essen → Iss!
Germans say 'eat with knife and fork'. Genders to learn: das Messer (knife), die Gabel (fork), der Löffel (spoon).
A German idiom: 'eat your plate empty'. leer = empty, and it goes at the end.
Schmeckt's? is short for Schmeckt es? (Does it taste good?). Answer: Ja, schmeckt super!
wer = who. Wer will ...? = Who wants ...? will is from wollen and means want, not 'will'.

phrases.en: Can you pass me the bread?
phrases.de: Gibst du mir mal das Brot?
phrases.ph: geepst doo meer mahl das broht
phrases.note: das Brot = bread (a das word). A bread roll is das Brötchen, a breakfast favourite in Germany.
aufhören = to stop. Hör auf! on its own means 'Stop it!'; add zu + verb to say what to stop doing.
Willst du ...? is more direct than Möchtest du ...? (would you like). Both are fine in a family.
Bist du fertig? = Are you done? Germans use it for food, homework or getting ready: Ich bin fertig! = I'm done!
bis = until. After bis, the verb (sind) is kicked to the end of the sentence.
Nimm! comes from nehmen (to take): Germans say 'take the fork' rather than 'use'. die Gabel = fork.
das Gemüse (vegetables) is singular in German, so it's dein Gemüse, not deine.
weg = away/gone. Short commands often drop the verb: Handys weg! Hände weg! (Hands off!)

phrases.de: Hör auf, mit dem Essen zu spielen!
phrases.ph: hur owf, mit daym E-sen tsoo SHPEE-len
phrases.note: Pattern: Hör auf, ... zu + verb! The comma is needed and zu spielen goes at the very end.
Sei! is the command of sein (to be). wählerisch = fussy, from wählen (to choose).
in Ordnung = fine, OK (literally 'in order'). völlig = completely. Alles in Ordnung? = Is everything OK?

phrases.de: Iss und hör auf zu meckern!
phrases.ph: is unt hur owf tsoo ME-kern
phrases.note: meckern = to moan or grumble. It's also the sound a goat makes. A bit blunt, but normal between parent and child.

phrases.de: Wir sind hier nicht im Restaurant!
phrases.ph: veer zint heer nisht im res-toh-RONG
phrases.note: Germans say 'we're not in a restaurant here'. im is short for in dem.
Sitz! is the command of sitzen (to sit), and still means still/quiet. Warning: Sitz! alone is what you say to Monty.

phrases.de: Hör auf, deinen Bruder zu treten!
phrases.ph: hur owf, DYE-nen BROO-der tsoo TRAY-ten
phrases.note: treten = to kick. der Bruder becomes deinen Bruder here. For a sister: deine Schwester.

phrases.en: Don't feed Monty under the table.
phrases.note: füttern is only for feeding animals or babies. unterm is short for unter dem (under the).
Kau! is from kauen (to chew). Kaugummi = chewing gum. After mit, geschlossen gets the ending -em.
abwischen = to wipe off. In a command it splits: Wisch ... ab! Again Germans say dir den Mund, not deinen.

phrases.en: Say thank you for the food.
phrases.note: sich bedanken für = to say thank you for. dich (yourself) is part of the verb, so it's 'thank yourself' in German.

phrases.de: Nicht über den Tisch greifen, frag lieber!
phrases.ph: nisht EW-ber dayn tish GRY-fen, frahk LEE-ber
phrases.note: Parents often give orders as nicht + verb: Nicht greifen! lieber = rather, so frag lieber = better ask.
abräumen = to clear away. It splits in a command: Räum ... ab, with bitte squeezed in near the front.
Germans praise food with schmecken (to taste): Das schmeckt super! = That tastes great!
German kids ask 'may I get up?' aufstehen = to get up. With darf ich it stays in one piece at the end.
scharf means both spicy and sharp (like a knife). Mild is the opposite for food.
der Nachtisch = dessert (literally 'after-table'). False friend: der Pudding is only a custard-like dessert.

phrases.en: Can I have a bit less?
phrases.de: Kann ich ein bisschen weniger haben?
phrases.ph: kan ish ine BIS-shen VAY-ni-ger HAH-ben
phrases.note: weniger = less, the opposite of mehr (more). ein bisschen weniger = a bit less.
Das schmeckt mir nicht = I don't like the taste of this. For food, it's more natural than Das mag ich nicht.
hassen = to hate. Just as blunt as in English, so expect a telling-off from whoever cooked.
eklig = disgusting, gross. It comes from der Ekel (disgust). Rude-ish if the cook hears it.
Igitt! is the German 'Yuck!' or 'Ew!'. Say it on its own when something looks or smells gross.

phrases.en: Why do we keep having this?
phrases.de: Warum gibt es das schon wieder?
phrases.ph: va-RUM geept es das shohn VEE-der
phrases.note: schon wieder = yet again, and it sounds annoyed. Warum gibt es das ...? = Why is there this ...?
Nicht schon wieder! is the classic moan, the same as 'Not again!'. Works for food, chores or homework.
kriegen = to get. It's casual and fine at home. Careful: bekommen also means get, not 'become'.
Ich kann nicht mehr = I can't (eat) any more. It also means 'I can't go on' when you're exhausted.
jetzt = now. Kann ich jetzt gehen? = Can I go now? Add bitte to sound less impatient.
ja here doesn't mean yes. It adds surprise or complaint: Das ist ja kalt! = But this is cold!
denn in a question adds curiosity or suspicion, like 'What on earth is this?' It doesn't mean 'then' here.
lecker = tasty, yummy. On its own, Lecker! is the German 'Yum!'
Ketchup can be der or das in German; both are correct. No word for 'some' is needed.
Sag ihm, er soll ... = Tell him he should ... For a girl: Sag ihr, sie soll aufhören!
nachmachen = to copy someone. It splits, so nach goes to the end. For a girl: Sie macht mich nach!
mehr als = more than. German uses ich here, not mich: mehr als ich. For a girl: Sie hat mehr als ich!
fair is borrowed from English. Also common: Das ist gemein! (That's mean!), gemein meaning mean or unfair.
Vegetarierin is a female vegetarian; a boy says Vegetarier. Germans use the noun here with no word for "a".

phrases.en: Do I have to eat all of it?
phrases.note: aufessen means to eat up, finish your plate. After muss (have to) the second verb waits at the very end, in its full form.
ein bisschen = a little bit. It works for anything: ein bisschen Soße, ein bisschen müde (a bit tired).
Es gibt means "there is", so Was gibt's? = what is there? Nachtisch is literally "after-table" – dessert.

phrases.en: Can I have it with nothing on it?
phrases.de: Kann ich das ohne alles haben?
phrases.ph: kan ish das OH-nuh A-les HAH-ben
phrases.note: ohne alles = without everything, the German way to say plain. You'll hear it ordering a burger or a Döner too.
war's is short for war es (was it). Germans say in der Schule (in the school) where we just say "at school".
der Tag (day) is masculine, but dein doesn't change here because Tag is the subject. Word for word: how was your day.
Spoken German uses the "have done" form for the past: hast ... gemacht. The gemacht part always goes to the end.
passieren (to happen) uses ist, not hat, in the past. After irgendwas (anything), the adjective becomes a noun: Interessantes, with a capital I.
aufhaben is everyday German for "to have homework set". The auf splits off and lands at the end of the question.
Hausaufgaben is Haus (house) + Aufgaben (tasks). It's nearly always plural, so it's deine, not dein.

phrases.de: Bis wann musst du das abgeben?
phrases.ph: bis van must doo das AP-gay-ben
phrases.note: Bis wann? = by when? abgeben means to hand in; after musst it stays in one piece at the end.
fertig = finished or ready. damit means "with it", so the whole thing is literally "Are you ready with it?"
brauchen = to need. German doesn't need a word for "any" here – just Hilfe (help), with a capital H because it's a noun.

phrases.en: Have you got a test tomorrow?
phrases.note: Germans "write" a test: einen Test schreiben. A bigger written test in class is a Klassenarbeit.
lernen covers learning, studying and revising. There's no separate everyday word for revise, so gelernt does the job.

phrases.en: What lesson have you got first?
phrases.de: Was hast du in der ersten Stunde?
phrases.ph: vas hast doo in dayr AYR-sten SHTUN-duh
phrases.note: Stunde means hour, but at school it's a lesson period. in der ersten Stunde = in the first period.
Schluss = end. Schluss haben is how you say school's over for you. Schluss jetzt! also means "That's enough now!"
Soll ich ...? = Shall I ...? – a handy way to offer anything. abholen (to pick up/collect) sits whole at the end.

phrases.en: Where should I pick you up?
phrases.note: dich = you (as the one being picked up). Compare du, which is "you" doing the action: Du holst mich ab.

phrases.en: What time should I pick you up?
phrases.de: Um wie viel Uhr soll ich dich abholen?
phrases.ph: um vee feel oor zol ish dish AP-hoh-len
phrases.note: Um wie viel Uhr? = at what time? Uhr is both clock and o'clock: um drei Uhr = at three o'clock.

phrases.de: Schreib mir, wenn du fertig bist.
phrases.ph: shripe meer, ven doo FER-tish bist
phrases.note: wenn (when) kicks the verb to the end: du bist fertig becomes wenn du fertig bist. Schreib mir = write to me, i.e. text me.

phrases.en: Let me know when you're ready.
phrases.de: Sag Bescheid, wenn du so weit bist.
phrases.ph: zahk be-SHITE, ven doo zoh vite bist
phrases.note: Sag Bescheid is the go-to phrase for "let me know". so weit sein = to be ready (literally "to be that far").
In commands, nicht comes at the end: Vergiss ... nicht! PE is just Sport in German, and Sachen means things or stuff.
packen = to pack, and gepackt is the past form. die Tasche (bag) is feminine, so it's deine Tasche.

phrases.en: Do you need anything for tomorrow?
phrases.de: Brauchst du noch was für morgen?
phrases.ph: browkhst doo nokh vas fewr MOR-gen
phrases.note: noch was = anything else, still something. was is short for etwas (something) in everyday speech.
Mach! is the du command from machen. zuerst = first; you'll often hear the shorter erst: Erst die Hausaufgaben!

phrases.en: What have you got to do?
phrases.note: müssen = must/have to. Pattern: Was musst du ...? = What do you have to ...? with the second verb at the end.
laufen means to run or walk, but also "to go" for how things turn out. Like most movement verbs, it uses ist in the past.
Watch out: bekommen means to get, NOT become. die Note = mark; in Germany 1 is the best and 6 the worst.
Word for word: good done. Swap gut for super or toll to sound even prouder: Super gemacht!

phrases.en: Who did you have lunch with?
phrases.de: Mit wem hast du zu Mittag gegessen?
phrases.ph: mit vaym hast doo tsoo MI-tahk ge-GE-sen
phrases.note: Mit wem? = with whom? After mit, wer (who) changes to wem. zu Mittag essen = to have lunch (Mittag = midday).
Freundinnen = female friends (male or mixed: Freunden). Wie geht's ...? asks how it goes for them, so the word takes the "to them" form.

phrases.de: Zeig mal, was du gemacht hast.
phrases.ph: tsike mahl, vas doo ge-MAKHT hast
phrases.note: mal softens a command, a bit like "just". After was (what) the verb hast moves to the end.

phrases.en: Put your books in your bag.
phrases.de: Pack deine Bücher in die Tasche.
phrases.ph: pak DYE-nuh BEW-sher in dee TA-shuh
phrases.note: Buch (book) becomes Bücher in the plural – the u gets dots and -er is added. Germans say "the bag", not "your bag".

phrases.en: Don't leave it till the last minute.
phrases.de: Schieb das nicht bis zur letzten Minute auf.
phrases.ph: sheep das nisht bis tsoor LETS-ten mi-NOO-tuh owf
phrases.note: aufschieben = to put off. The schieb goes near the start and the auf jumps to the very end of the sentence.
kein/keine means "no" or "not any" in front of a noun – use it instead of nicht. hab is the chatty short form of habe.
schon = already. hab's squashes habe es (have it) into one word, which is how people really talk.
Casual German drops das from the start: (Das) mach ich später. The present tense works for the future here.

phrases.en: I need help with my homework.
phrases.de: Ich brauche Hilfe bei den Hausaufgaben.
phrases.ph: ish BROW-khuh HIL-fuh by dayn HOWS-owf-gah-ben
phrases.note: Help with something is Hilfe bei, not mit. bei den = with the – German prefers "the" to "my" here.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: helfen takes mir (to me), not mich: you give help TO someone. dabei = with it/with this.
Starting with Das puts the stress on "this". The verb verstehe must still be the second thing, so ich comes after it.
drüberschauen = to look over something quickly. drüber is short for darüber (over it). A handy one before handing work in.
ausdrucken = to print out. With muss it stays whole at the end; on its own it splits: Ich drucke das aus.
gehen means to go, but also "to work" for machines: Das Handy geht nicht. der Drucker (printer) comes from drucken, to print.

phrases.en: I need something for school tomorrow.
phrases.de: Ich brauche morgen was für die Schule.
phrases.ph: ish BROW-khuh MOR-gen vas fewr dee SHOO-luh
phrases.note: German likes time words early: morgen comes before what you need. Remember morgen = tomorrow, but der Morgen = the morning.
vergessen (to forget) has no ge- added in the past, because it already starts with ver-. Chatty speech drops the das at the start.

phrases.de: Ich brauche Geld für die Schule.
phrases.ph: ish BROW-khuh gelt fewr dee SHOO-luh
phrases.note: das Geld = money. Careful: Gold is gold, and Geld is never plural – it's always just Geld.

phrases.en: I need you to sign this.
phrases.note: unterschreiben = to sign (under + write). This unter never splits off: Ich unterschreibe, not Ich schreibe unter.
der Test is masculine, so "a test" becomes einen Test when it's the thing being written.

phrases.en: I don't want to go to school.
phrases.de: Ich will nicht in die Schule.
phrases.ph: ish vil nisht in dee SHOO-luh
phrases.note: ich will = I want (not "I will" – a false friend!). The word gehen is often left out: in die Schule is enough.
müde = tired. Add total or voll for teen emphasis: Ich bin total müde.
langweilig = boring, from lang (long) + Weile (a while) – time drags. Mir ist langweilig = I'm bored.
ganz okay = alright, fine. ganz usually means "quite" or "whole", so ganz okay sounds a bit shrugging – perfect here.
nichts = nothing. passieren uses ist in the past, so it's ist ... passiert, with passiert at the end.
wissen (to know facts) is odd: ich weiß, with no -e and a ß. Dropping das at the start makes it sound nicely offhand.
nicht mehr = no longer, not any more. So "I don't know any more" is how Germans say they can't remember.
German uses one negative: nichts on its own means "not anything". Never add nicht as well.
Kannst du ...? = Can you ...? It's the easiest way to ask a favour – the action verb goes to the end.

phrases.en: Can you pick me up early?
phrases.note: früher means earlier (than planned). früh = early; früher also means "in the past" in other sentences.

phrases.en: What time are you picking me up?
phrases.note: Without kannst or soll, abholen splits: holst at the front, ab right at the end.
abfragen = to test someone by asking questions, e.g. on vocab. fragen alone just means to ask.
German says "I have to hand it in tomorrow". abgeben (to hand in) also means to give away.

phrases.de: Ich hab eine gute Note bekommen.
phrases.ph: ish hahp EYE-nuh GOO-tuh NOH-tuh be-KO-men
phrases.note: die Note is feminine, so "a good" is eine gute. bekommen = to get – never to become.
bestehen = to pass a test or exam. The past form is bestanden, with no ge- because of the be- start.
durchfallen = to fail, literally "to fall through". Falling is movement, so it takes bin, not hab.
Ich muss ... = I have to .... Here lernen means revise. Be careful: Ich muss nicht means I don't have to, not I mustn't.
Darf ich ...? = Am I allowed to ...? – politer than kann ich. The verb (go) is dropped: "May I on the computer?"
nachsitzen = to have detention, literally "to sit after". German uses a verb where English uses a noun.
Schulausflug = Schule + Ausflug (trip). In joined-up nouns, the last word decides the gender: der Ausflug, so einen.
German skips the "and": Geh + aufräumen (to tidy up) = go tidy. das Zimmer means room; Schlafzimmer is bedroom but rarely needed.

phrases.de: Dein Zimmer ist ein einziges Chaos.
phrases.ph: dine TSI-mer ist ine INE-tsi-ges KAH-os
phrases.note: ein einziges Chaos = one big mess (einzig = single, only). das Chaos is a noun, so it's capitalised.
With split verbs like aufräumen, the ge- slides into the middle for the past: auf-ge-räumt.
aufheben = to pick up. As a command it splits: Heb ... auf! Careful – aufheben can also mean to keep or save something.
wegräumen = to clear away (weg = away). In the command, weg jumps to the end: Räum das weg!
Klamotten is the casual word for clothes, like "gear". The proper word is Kleidung, which you'd write in an essay.

phrases.en: Put your dirty clothes in the wash.
phrases.de: Tu deine schmutzige Wäsche in den Wäschekorb.
phrases.ph: too DYE-nuh SHMUT-si-guh VE-shuh in dayn VE-shuh-korp
phrases.note: die Wäsche = the washing/laundry; der Wäschekorb = laundry basket. tun (to do) is also everyday German for "to put".
sauber = clean (it doesn't mean sour – that's sauer!). dreckig = dirty, a bit stronger than schmutzig.

phrases.en: Don't leave it on the floor.
phrases.de: Lass das nicht auf dem Boden liegen.
phrases.ph: las das nisht owf daym BOH-den LEE-gen
phrases.note: liegen lassen = to leave lying around. Germans say what the thing is doing: it lies, so liegen goes at the end.
Easy one: machen = to make, and das Bett = the bed. Same idea as English, word for word.
aufmachen = to open (literally make open). Vorhänge (curtains) comes from vor (in front) + hängen (to hang).
das Fenster (window) is neuter, and the plural is the same: die Fenster. You can also say öffnen, but aufmachen is more chatty.
zumachen is the opposite of aufmachen: auf = open, zu = shut. Swap the little word at the end to flip the meaning.
die Tür (door) is feminine. You'll also hear Tür zu! on its own – short, sharp and very common.
lassen = to leave or let. Lass is its du command form. offen = open, as a describing word.
ausmachen = to switch off; the aus goes to the end. Same pattern for the TV: Mach den Fernseher aus!
anmachen = to switch on – just swap aus for an. das Licht = the light.
runter is short for herunter (down). Add it to a verb: runterbringen = bring down, runterkommen = come down.

phrases.de: Kannst du das nach oben bringen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo das nahkh OH-ben BRING-en
phrases.note: nach oben = upstairs (to the top). Its opposite is nach unten. oben on its own means "up there".

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.de: Kannst du mir hier mal helfen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer heer mahl HEL-fen
phrases.note: hier mal adds "here, for a sec" and makes the request sound casual. helfen always goes with mir, not mich.
mit anpacken = to lend a hand, literally "grab on with". Both mit and an go to the end in the command.
gehören = to belong to. German asks "To whom does this belong?", so it's Wem, not Wessen.
deins = yours (for a das word). Pattern: meins = mine, deins = yours – Das ist meins! is a classic sibling line.
hingehören = to belong somewhere. Wo ... hin? asks where to, with hin moving to the end.

phrases.de: Kannst du in deinem Zimmer staubsaugen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo in DYE-nem TSI-mer SHTOWP-zow-gen
phrases.note: staubsaugen = to hoover, from Staub (dust) + saugen (to suck). in deinem Zimmer = in your room.
Germans "re-cover the bed": das Bett neu beziehen. There's no need for a separate word for sheets.
das Handtuch = towel (literally hand cloth). aufhängen splits in the command: Häng ... auf!
der Müll = rubbish, so it's den Müll here. Germans sort it into different bins, so you may hear which one: den Biomüll.

phrases.en: Can you hang the washing out?
phrases.note: aufhängen works for towels and washing alike. Many German families dry clothes on a Wäscheständer (clothes horse).
reinholen = to fetch in. holen (to fetch) + rein (in, short for herein), and rein goes to the end.
zusammenlegen = to fold, literally "lay together". Sachen (things) is a common way to say clothes at home.
stinken = to stink, and it's blunt. riechen is the neutral "to smell": Hier riecht's gut = It smells nice here.

phrases.en: There are dirty cups in your room.
phrases.de: In deinem Zimmer stehen dreckige Tassen.
phrases.ph: in DYE-nem TSI-mer SHTAY-en DRE-ki-guh TA-sen
phrases.note: German says cups "stand" (stehen) rather than "there are". Things upright stand; flat things lie (liegen).
dran sein = to be someone's turn. Wer ist dran? = Whose turn is it? Du bist dran! = Your turn!
gestern = yesterday. The heute/gestern/morgen trio (today/yesterday/tomorrow) is worth knowing by heart.
doch here means "but it IS" – it pushes back against what the parent just said. Classic arguing word.

phrases.de: Hör auf, ständig in mein Zimmer zu gehen!
phrases.ph: hur owf, SHTEN-dish in mine TSI-mer tsoo GAY-en
phrases.note: Hör auf, ... zu ...! = Stop doing ...! The zu + verb goes at the end. ständig = constantly.
anfassen = to touch. In the command, nicht and an stack up at the end: Fass ... nicht an!
danach = after that; gleich = straight away. Together they mean "right after this" – the teen's favourite delay.
German happily drops the verb in complaints: "Why always I?" warum = why, immer = always.
doch adds "I told you!" annoyance. Without it, the sentence is just a plain fact.
der Staubsauger = hoover, literally "dust sucker". Joined-up nouns take the gender of the last part: der Sauger.

phrases.en: It's his turn to empty the dishwasher.
phrases.de: Er ist dran, die Spülmaschine auszuräumen.
phrases.ph: ayr ist dran, dee SHPEWL-ma-shee-nuh OWS-tsoo-roy-men
phrases.note: ausräumen = to empty/unload; the zu squeezes into the middle: auszuräumen. For a sister, swap Er for Sie.
gefallen = to please, so German says "It pleases me like this". That's why it starts with Mir, not Ich.
After wo (where) in the middle of a sentence, the verb ist goes to the end: wo alles ist.
anklopfen = to knock (on a door). Klopf goes first and an goes last, with erst (first) in between.
Word order matters: Räum + thing + nicht + auf. The auf of aufräumen always comes after the nicht.

phrases.en: Where did you put my hoodie?
phrases.de: Wo hast du meinen Hoodie hingelegt?
phrases.ph: voh hast doo MY-nen HOO-dee HIN-ge-laykt
phrases.note: German borrowed Hoodie and made it masculine: der Hoodie, so "my" becomes meinen here. hinlegen = to put down somewhere.

phrases.de: Jetzt finde ich gar nichts mehr.
phrases.ph: yetst FIN-duh ish gahr nishts mayr
phrases.note: gar nichts = nothing at all; mehr adds "any more". Starting with Jetzt pushes ich after the verb.

phrases.de: Boah, na gut, ich komm ja schon.
phrases.ph: BOH-ah, nah goot, ish kom yah shohn
phrases.note: na gut = oh alright. ja schon adds "I'm coming, OK!" impatience. Boah is a big sigh – very teen.
nicht goes before the describing word it cancels: nicht dreckig. Say doch nicht dreckig to argue harder.
hab ... gemacht = have made. Chatty German cuts habe to hab – you'll hear it far more than the full form.

phrases.en: Why do I have to do everything?
phrases.note: No "do" helper word in German questions: just flip the verb and ich – muss ich. alles = everything.
heißen means to be called, but also "to mean". Note the German quote marks: low at the start, high at the end.

phrases.en: I don't care whose it is.
phrases.de: Mir ist egal, wem das gehört.
phrases.ph: meer ist ay-GAHL, vaym das ge-HURT
phrases.note: Mir ist egal = I don't care (literally "to me it's the same"). After wem, gehört goes to the end.
die Ausrede = excuse; plural Ausreden. keine is the "no" you put in front of nouns.
Komm mir nicht mit ... = don't come at me with ... — handy for shutting down any excuse. „egal“ is the German shrug word: whatever.

phrases.en: Don't roll your eyes at me.
phrases.note: verdrehen = to twist or roll. die Augen (the eyes) is plural, which always takes die. German doesn't need the 'at me' part.
After weil (because) the verb jumps to the end: weil ich es sage. The classic no-arguments parent line.

phrases.en: You said that an hour ago.
phrases.de: Das hast du vor einer Stunde auch schon gesagt.
phrases.ph: das hast doo fohr EYE-ner SHTUN-duh owkh shohn ge-ZAHKT
phrases.note: vor einer Stunde = an hour ago. With time, vor means 'ago' and comes before the time, not after it like in English.
noch mal = again, once more — you'll hear it all the time. The careful written form is noch einmal.
Widerworte literally 'against-words' = backchat. wider means against, as in widersprechen (to contradict).
zählen = to count, bis = up to. Watch the umlaut: zahlen without it means to pay.
sondern = but (rather), used after nicht to correct something. gleich is the German 'in a minute'.

phrases.en: You're not busy, you're on your phone.
phrases.de: Du bist nicht beschäftigt, du hängst am Handy.
phrases.ph: doo bist nisht be-SHEF-tisht, doo hengst am HEN-dee
phrases.note: am Handy hängen = to be glued to your phone (literally 'hang on the phone'). Handy looks English, but only Germans use it for a mobile.

phrases.en: I don't care who did it.
phrases.de: Mir ist egal, wer es war.
phrases.ph: meer ist ay-GAHL, vayr es vahr
phrases.note: Mir ist egal = I don't care (literally 'to me it's all the same'). After wer (who) as a linking word, the verb war goes last.

phrases.en: If you know, why haven't you done it?
phrases.de: Wenn du es weißt, warum hast du es dann nicht gemacht?
phrases.ph: ven doo es vyst, va-RUM hast doo es dan nisht ge-MAKHT
phrases.note: weißt is from wissen (to know a fact). After wenn (if) the verb goes to the end of that part: wenn du es weißt.

phrases.de: Und warum ist es dann noch nicht erledigt?
phrases.ph: unt va-RUM ist es dan nokh nisht er-LAY-disht
phrases.note: erledigt = done, sorted — the go-to word for finished jobs. Ist das erledigt? = Is that done?
der Versuch = attempt, from versuchen (to try). Because it's a der word, nett picks up -er: Netter Versuch.
aufhören (to stop) splits into Hör auf! Add zu + a verb to say what to stop: zu schnaufen = huffing.
kennen = to know something familiar (a person, a story). Putting die Ausrede first stresses it, but kenne still sits second.
Literally 'tell me nothing' — really 'don't give me that'. The little word doch adds an annoyed 'oh come on' tone.
erfinden = to invent, so 'stop inventing excuses'. die Ausrede (excuse) keeps its capital A even mid-sentence, like all nouns.
German often uses the present for the future: ich mach das später = I'll do it later. mach is spoken short for mache.

phrases.en: I'll do it in a minute.
phrases.note: gleich = in a minute, right away. mach's squashes mache + es together, a bit like English 'I'll'.

phrases.en: I was going to do it!
phrases.note: Ich wollte gerade ... = I was just about to ... wollte is the past of wollen (to want); machen goes to the end.
Ich weiß is from wissen (to know a fact). That ß is a sharp double-s letter — don't write it as a B.

phrases.de: Das hast du mir schon gesagt.
phrases.ph: das hast doo meer shohn ge-ZAHKT
phrases.note: schon = already. In the past form hast ... gesagt, hast sits second and gesagt goes right to the end.
hab is spoken short for habe. gehört = heard, from hören — not to be confused with gehören (to belong).
ja schon adds 'I'm already on it, OK?!' — pure teen irritation. German has no -ing form: ich mache = I do / I'm doing.
Warte! is the command to one person. To several people it's Wartet! Adding mal (Warte mal!) makes it softer.
Moment mal! = hang on. mal here is a softening word Germans put in requests — it doesn't mean 'times'.
die Sekunde is a die word, so 'one' becomes eine. You'll also hear just Sekunde! on its own.
Warum? = why. Wieso? means exactly the same and sounds a bit more casual — both are used at home.

phrases.en: Why do I have to do it?
phrases.note: muss is from müssen (to have to). With muss in the sentence, the second verb machen goes to the very end.

phrases.de: Warum kann er das nicht machen?
phrases.ph: va-RUM kan ayr das nisht MA-khen
phrases.note: er = he; for a sister it's sie. The verb kann sits second, and machen waits at the very end after nicht.
meins = mine, used on its own without a noun. Das gehört mir nicht ('that doesn't belong to me') means the same.
In speech Germans use this past form: hab ... gemacht. nicht slots in just before gemacht at the end.
Literally 'that was I not'. Putting ich before nicht stresses it — it wasn't ME.

phrases.de: Ich hab das nicht da liegen lassen.
phrases.ph: ish hahp das nisht dah LEE-gen LA-sen
phrases.note: liegen lassen = to leave lying about. Germans say where things lie (liegen) for flat things and stand (stehen) for upright ones.
aufräumen = to tidy up. It splits in a normal sentence: ich räum das später auf — the auf jumps to the end.

phrases.de: So schlimm ist mein Zimmer gar nicht.
phrases.ph: zoh shlim ist mine TSI-mer gahr nisht
phrases.note: gar nicht = not at all. Starting with So schlimm pushes ist into second place, ahead of mein Zimmer.
finden = to find. Watch out: ich finde also means 'I think' (Ich finde das gut = I think it's good).
Literally 'where does this come to?' The hin shows movement towards a place — Wohin? means 'where to?'

phrases.en: What do you want me to do?
phrases.note: soll is from sollen (to be supposed to): Was soll ich machen? = what should I do? denn adds an exasperated tone.
Muss ich? works on its own — no 'do it' needed. The extra-whiny version is Muss das sein? (Must that be?).

phrases.de: Ich hab das gestern schon gemacht.
phrases.ph: ish hahp das GES-tern shohn ge-MAKHT
phrases.note: gestern = yesterday (heute = today, morgen = tomorrow). The schon ('already') makes the excuse sound stronger.
dran sein = to be someone's turn. Er ist dran = it's his turn; for a sister, Sie ist dran.
Wer ist dran? (whose turn is it?) is the question you'll hear before every chore — this is the reply.
immer = always. To moan even harder, just say Immer ich! — 'always me!'
beschäftigt = busy. The more casual Ich hab zu tun ('I've got things to do') is just as common.
Ich bin fertig! = I've finished. Careful: it can also mean 'I'm shattered', so context matters.
sauber = clean; the opposite is dreckig (dirty). Starting with Jetzt sends ist into second place.
Kann ich ...? = Can I ...? The other verb goes last: Kann ich das morgen machen? Swap in any verb you like.

phrases.en: What do I get for it?
phrases.note: kriegen = to get (casual). The neater word is bekommen — a false friend: it means get, never become.
die Schuld = fault or blame. Because Schuld is a die word, 'my' becomes meine.
weglegen = to put away or down. In a command it splits: Leg ... weg! with the weg at the end.
Schluss = end. Schluss mit ...! means 'enough of ...!' and works for anything: Schluss mit dem Streit!

phrases.en: How long have you been on your phone?
phrases.de: Wie lange hängst du schon am Handy?
phrases.ph: vee LANG-uh hengst doo shohn am HEN-dee
phrases.note: Wie lange ... schon? + present tense = how long have you been ...? German uses the present where English says 'have been'.
leiser = quieter, from leise. Mach ... leiser / lauter = turn ... down / up — works for music, TV, anything.
Mach leiser! is all you need — German drops the 'it' here. Mach is the command form of machen (to make/do).
zu here means too, not to: zu laut = too loud, zu spät = too late.
Kopfhörer = headphones, literally 'head listeners'. You put them on with aufsetzen, so the auf goes to the end.
der Fernseher = the TV set. It becomes den here because it's the thing being acted on.
gucken = to watch or look — the everyday word at home. The textbook version is Was schaust du? or Was siehst du?
spielen = to play (games, sport, music). German has no separate 'are playing' form: Was spielst du? covers it.
Mit wem? = with whom? In German you always talk mit someone, and the mit comes first. reden = to talk.
immer noch = still. Germans also turn apps into verbs, just like English: facetimen, googeln.
aufladen = to charge. After musst, the verb stays in one piece at the end: dein Handy aufladen.
das Ladegerät = charger (Lade = charging, Gerät = device). German glues words together to build long nouns.

phrases.en: Don't forget to charge your phone.
phrases.note: With a splitting verb like aufladen, zu slips into the middle: aufzuladen. Vergiss nicht = don't forget.
die Bildschirmzeit = screen time (Bildschirm = screen). genug = enough, and it goes before the noun, as in English.

phrases.de: Es ist Zeit, Schluss zu machen.
phrases.ph: es ist tsite, shlus tsoo MA-khen
phrases.note: Schluss machen = to stop, wrap up. Careful: said to a boyfriend or girlfriend it means to break up!

phrases.de: Noch fünf Minuten, dann ist Schluss.
phrases.ph: nokh fewnf mi-NOO-ten, dan ist shlus
phrases.note: noch here means more: noch fünf Minuten = five more minutes. Put noch before any amount: noch ein Stück = one more piece.

phrases.en: No, I'm not extending your time limit.
phrases.de: Nein, ich verlängere deine Zeit nicht.
phrases.ph: nine, ish fer-LENG-e-ruh DYE-nuh tsite nisht
phrases.note: verlängern = to extend — it contains lang (long), so 'to make longer'. nicht at the end cancels the whole idea.

phrases.en: Why do you need more time?
phrases.note: Wozu? = what for? — a sharper 'why' that asks for the purpose. brauchen = to need.
gönnen = to let someone have something nice, so 'treat your eyes to a break'. die Pause = break.
ausmachen = to turn off, anmachen = to turn on. In a command the aus goes right to the end.
die Fernbedienung = the remote, literally 'far control'. fern (far) is the same as in Fernseher.
wem = to whom. You write to someone, so it's wem, not wen. Mit wem schreibst du? is also common.
der Computer is the same word as in English, just with a capital C because all nouns get one. Also heard: der Rechner.

phrases.de: Lass dein Handy heute Nacht unten.
phrases.ph: las dine HEN-dee HOY-tuh nakht UN-ten
phrases.note: unten = downstairs (literally 'below'); oben = upstairs. heute Nacht = tonight.

phrases.en: Can you turn it up a bit?
phrases.de: Kannst du es ein bisschen lauter machen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo es ine BIS-shen LOW-ter MA-khen
phrases.note: ein bisschen = a bit — hugely common. Kannst du ...? = Can you ...?, with the other verb (machen) at the end.
teilen = to share (and to divide in maths). im is short for in dem: im Internet = online.

phrases.en: Look at me, not your phone.
phrases.de: Schau mich an, nicht aufs Handy!
phrases.ph: show mish an, nisht owfs HEN-dee
phrases.note: anschauen (to look at) splits: Schau mich an! aufs is short for auf das — 'at the phone'.
das Handy is a das word, so 'my' is just mein. Germans never call a mobile a Mobile — it's always Handy.
Hast du ... gesehen? = Have you seen ...? Reuse it for anything: Hast du meine Schuhe gesehen?
anrufen = to ring. German just says 'ring me' — no 'my phone'. The mal makes the request sound casual.
leer = empty, so a dead phone is 'empty'. You can also say Mein Akku ist leer (my battery's flat).
In a glued-together noun the last part decides der/die/das: das Gerät, so das Ladegerät and plain mein.
das Ladekabel = charging cable, what many Germans call the charger. Kabel = cable, just spelt with a K.

phrases.de: Kann ich mir dein Ladegerät ausleihen?
phrases.ph: kan ish meer dine LAH-duh-ge-rayt OWS-lye-en
phrases.note: sich etwas ausleihen = to borrow something. mir means 'for myself'; ausleihen stays whole at the end after kann.
Germans say WLAN for Wi-Fi. Wie ist ...? (literally 'how is') is how you ask for a password, name or number.
gehen means to go, but ... geht nicht is the everyday way to say something isn't working.
total = really, totally — teens use it constantly. langsam = slow; schnell = fast.

phrases.en: Can you turn off the time limit?
phrases.note: ausschalten = to switch off. After Kannst du, it stays in one piece at the end instead of splitting.

phrases.de: Kann ich noch mehr Zeit haben?
phrases.ph: kan ish nokh mayr tsite HAH-ben
phrases.note: noch mehr = some more. For a casual version try Krieg ich noch Zeit? (can I get more time?).
Nur noch = just ... more. The noch matters: nur fünf Minuten on its own means 'only five minutes'.
sperren = to block or lock. gesperrt is its past form, parked at the end of the sentence.

phrases.de: Ich brauche das für die Schule.
phrases.ph: ish BROW-khuh das fewr dee SHOO-luh
phrases.note: für die Schule = for school. German needs the die here, where English just says 'school'.
Freundinnen = female friends; for male or mixed friends say meinen Freunden. After mit, meine gets an extra -n.
gleich fertig = nearly done, literally 'finished in a moment'. The perfect stalling line.

phrases.en: Wait, I'm just replying to someone.
phrases.note: gerade = right now — German's way of saying 'I'm in the middle of'. You answer to someone, so it's jemandem.
fast is a false friend: it means almost, not quick. der Akku = phone battery.
benutzen = to use. Swap Kann ich for Darf ich (may I) to sound more polite when asking a parent.

phrases.de: Kannst du mir einen Hotspot machen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer EYE-nen HOT-spot MA-khen
phrases.note: der Hotspot is borrowed from English. As a der word it becomes einen when it's the thing being made.
kein ... mehr = no more ... — a really useful pattern. das Datenvolumen = your mobile data allowance.
springen usually means to jump, but gesprungen for glass or a screen means cracked. Germans say Display for a phone screen.

phrases.de: Darf ich mir diese App runterladen?
phrases.ph: darf ish meer DEE-zuh ep RUN-ter-lah-den
phrases.note: runterladen = to download (casual for herunterladen). die App is a die word, so 'this' becomes diese.
bekommen = to get — a classic false friend, it never means become. die Nachricht = message.
schicken = to send, dir = to you. der Link becomes den Link because it's the thing being sent.

phrases.de: Kannst du den Router neu starten?
phrases.ph: kanst doo dayn ROW-ter noy SHTAR-ten
phrases.note: neu starten = to restart, literally 'start new'. It's der Router, which turns into den here.
lesen changes its vowel in commands: Lies! (read!). Nachrichten also means 'the news'.

phrases.en: Can you top up my phone?
phrases.de: Kannst du mir Guthaben aufs Handy laden?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer GOOT-hah-ben owfs HEN-dee LAH-den
phrases.note: das Guthaben = credit (money on a phone or card). aufs is short for auf das — 'onto the phone'.

phrases.de: Hör auf, deinen Bruder zu nerven!
phrases.ph: hur owf, DYE-nen BROO-der tsoo NER-fen
phrases.note: nerven = to annoy, get on someone's nerves. For a sister: deine Schwester. Teen favourite: Nerv nicht!
in Ruhe lassen = to leave alone, literally 'leave in peace'. der Bruder becomes deinen Bruder here; a sister is deine Schwester.
Hört auf! is the command for several people (the ihr form ends in -t). To one person it's Hör auf!
Ihr beide = both of you. ihr is 'you' for more than one person, so the verb is hört.
passieren uses ist, not hat, in the past: Was ist passiert? Verbs about something happening or moving often do.
gemacht is the past of machen. Neutral question or accusation — in German it's all in your tone.
er = he (for a sister: sie). hat is the 'he/she' form of haben — hast is only for du.
jemandem die Schuld geben = to blame someone, literally 'give them the guilt'. ihm = to him; to her is ihr.
zurückgeben = to give back. Gib is the command of geben, and zurück jumps to the end.
gehören + person = to belong to. ihm = to him, so 'that belongs to him'.
ihr here means 'to her' — but the same word also means 'you lot'. Context tells you which.
After bevor (before) the verb goes last: bevor du es nimmst. nimmst is from nehmen (to take).
Sei! is the irregular command form of sein (to be). Reuse it: Sei leise! Sei vorsichtig!
ärgern = to wind someone up on purpose. ihn = him; for a sister, sie. With sich (sich ärgern) it means to get annoyed.
einfach = just, simply — it softens a command. ihn = him; for her, say Ignorier sie einfach!
Lass es! = leave it, drop it. lassen is a super-useful verb: to let, to leave, to stop doing.
From reichen (to be enough), literally 'it's enough'. The classic parent shout — Jetzt reicht's! is even crosser.

phrases.en: I don't care who started it.
phrases.de: Mir ist egal, wer angefangen hat.
phrases.ph: meer ist ay-GAHL, vayr AN-ge-fang-en hat
phrases.note: anfangen = to start. In the past form ge squeezes into the middle: angefangen. After wer, hat goes last.
Klärt is the ihr command of klären (to sort out). unter euch = between yourselves – ihr because it's said to both of you.
sich entschuldigen = to apologise. The dich (yourself) stays in the command – literally 'excuse yourself!'
ihm = to him (for a sister: ihr). der Freiraum = space, room to breathe.

phrases.en: Go away for five minutes and calm down.
phrases.de: Geh mal fünf Minuten raus und beruhig dich.
phrases.ph: gay mahl fewnf mi-NOO-ten rows unt be-ROO-ish dish
phrases.note: beruhig dich = calm down. sich beruhigen needs dich (yourself). raus = out, short for heraus.
Hör auf zu ... = Stop ...ing. Swap in any verb at the end: Hör auf zu jammern! (Stop moaning!)

phrases.en: Don't talk to him like that.
phrases.note: After mit, er (he) becomes ihm – for a sister it's mit ihr. Sprich is the du command of sprechen, e changing to i.
sich abwechseln = to take turns. It's a separable verb, so ab jumps to the end. Wechselt is the ihr form, for both of you.
teilen = to share. euch adds 'between you'. To just one person you'd say Teil das!
petzen = to tell tales, grass someone up. A telltale is eine Petze – a word German kids throw at each other.

phrases.en: You're both as bad as each other.
phrases.de: Ihr seid doch beide gleich schlimm!
phrases.ph: eer zite dokh BY-duh glyesh shlim
phrases.note: gleich schlimm = equally bad. gleich means 'the same' here, not 'in a minute' as in Ich komme gleich.
nett = nice, kind. Frag ihn = ask him (for a sister: Frag sie). No extra word needed, just like English.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, you two.
phrases.note: Seid is the ihr command of sein (to be). leiser = quieter: leise (quiet) + -er, just like quiet-er.

phrases.en: That's not how we talk to each other.
phrases.note: miteinander = with each other. Starting with So pushes the verb reden into second place, ahead of wir.
anfangen = to start. In the past tense the ge squeezes into the middle: an-ge-fangen. For a sister: Sie hat angefangen!
das Zimmer = room. When in describes where something is, mein changes to meinem.
Pattern: Sag ihm, er soll ... = Tell him he should ... (sister: Sag ihr, sie soll ...). soll sends aufhören to the end.
Raus! = Out! No verb needed. Very blunt – fine with a sibling, rude to anyone else.
nachmachen = to copy someone. With zu, the zu slips inside the verb: nach-zu-machen.
gehören = to belong. Das gehört mir is literally 'That belongs to me' – the usual way to say 'That's mine!'
fair is borrowed from English and sounds the same. For extra drama try Das ist ungerecht! (That's unjust!)
kriegen = to get (casual). der Wille = will, so seinen Willen kriegen = to get his way (hers: ihren Willen).
nerven = to get on your nerves. Er nervt! is how Germans say it – a verb, no adjective needed. total = totally.
nervig = annoying, from die Nerven (nerves). Blunt – fine with a sibling, not with a teacher.
die Ruhe = peace and quiet, so this is literally 'Leave me in peace!' A phrase worth learning whole.
German has no 'is ...ing' form: er nervt mich covers both 'he annoys me' and 'he is annoying me'.
geschlagen is the past form of schlagen (to hit). hat sits second and geschlagen goes to the very end.
zuerst = first. war is the past of sein (to be), so ich war = I was.
zurückgeben = to give back. In a command it splits: Gib ... zurück! with zurück jumping to the end.
Hör auf! comes from aufhören (to stop). The auf splits off and goes to the end. Hör auf damit! = Stop that!
Geh from gehen (to go) + weg (away). Short and blunt – fine with family, rude with guests.
angucken = to look at (casual). It's separable, so an jumps to the end: Er guckt mich an.
anfassen = to touch; die Sachen = things, stuff. The an goes right to the end, even after nicht.
lügen = to tell lies; eine Lüge = a lie. Don't mix it up with liegen = to lie down.
Literally 'Hold the flap!' – die Klappe is slang for your mouth. Rude: siblings only.
dran sein = to be someone's turn. Ich bin dran = my turn; Du bist dran = your turn.
das Ladekabel = charging cable (laden = to charge + Kabel). genommen is the past form of nehmen (to take).
so ein = such a. das Baby is borrowed straight from English, same spelling and meaning.
hab is the spoken short form of habe. angefasst is the past of anfassen (to touch). ihn = him; for a sister, sie.
Wo = where. Watch out: wer looks like 'where' but means who – a classic trap.
der Hund = the dog, with a capital H like every German noun. English 'hound' comes from the same word.
Pattern: Hast du ... gesehen? = Have you seen ...? What you've lost goes in the middle, gesehen at the end.
rauslassen = to let out. After Kannst du ...? (Can you ...?) the second verb goes to the very end.
reinlassen = to let in. der Hund becomes den Hund because the dog is the one being let in.
raus = out, rein = in. Swap that one little word at the end to flip the meaning.

phrases.en: Can you take Monty for a walk?
phrases.de: Kannst du mit Monty Gassi gehen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo mit MON-tee GA-see GAY-en
phrases.note: Gassi gehen = to walk the dog – a phrase used only for dogs. Literally you go 'with Monty' (mit Monty).

phrases.en: Has Monty been for a walk?
phrases.note: Literally 'Was Monty already outside?' schon = already/yet, and draußen = outside.
bekommen = to get, NOT to become – a famous false friend. das Futter = pet food.
füttern = to feed an animal, linked to das Futter (pet food). Feeding people uses different words.
der Hund is masculine, so the dog is 'he' in German too. ihm = to him. etwas = some.
der Wassernapf = Wasser (water) + Napf (bowl). German glues nouns together, and the last part decides der/die/das.
die Leine = lead. Because it's a die word, sein (his) gets an -e: seine Leine.
anlegen = to put on (a lead or collar). In the command, an jumps to the end. Germans say 'put him the lead on'.
ihn = him, when he's the one being let out. nicht comes just before raus at the very end.
zumachen = to shut, and zu jumps to the end. das Tor = gate – and also 'goal' in football.
rufen = to call out to someone. Careful: anrufen means to phone, so Ruf Monty an! would mean 'ring Monty'.
vom is short for von dem (off the). runter = down. das Sofa is the same word as in English.
Was = what – it's not the English 'was'. da = there, so it's really 'What has he got there?'
wegnehmen = to take away. Nimm ... weg! splits, and ihm means 'from him' here.
Hör auf, ... zu ... = Stop ...ing. The zu sits right before the verb at the end: ihn zu füttern.
Literally 'Don't give him that' – Germans use geben (give) here. nicht goes last in the sentence.
muss mal = needs to go (to the loo). The verb is simply left off because everyone knows. Works for people: Ich muss mal!
der Haufen = pile – the polite way to say dog poo. Mach ... weg = get rid of; weg goes to the end.
die Hundetüte = dog-poo bag (Hund + Tüte, bag). mitnehmen = to take with you, so mit goes to the end.
bellen = to bark; Warum = why. After a question word the verb comes straight next, then er.
die Pfote = paw, plural Pfoten. dreckig = dirty or muddy, from der Dreck (dirt).
abtrocknen = to dry off. German says 'dry him the paws': ihm (for him) plus die instead of seine.

phrases.en: Don't let him on the bed.
phrases.note: aufs is short for auf das (onto the). das Bett = bed – almost the same as English.

phrases.de: Hat er seine Tablette schon bekommen?
phrases.ph: hat ayr ZYE-nuh ta-BLE-tuh shohn be-KO-men
phrases.note: die Tablette = pill. The computer kind is das Tablet – different word, different gender.
Sitz! is the standard German dog command, from sitzen (to sit). German dogs also learn Platz! (lie down) and Aus! (drop).
das Leckerli = dog treat, from lecker (tasty). The -li ending makes it sound small and cute.
sich übergeben = to be sick. Without sich, übergeben means to hand over. The slangy version is gekotzt.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.de: Darf Monty in meinem Zimmer schlafen?
phrases.ph: darf MON-tee in MY-nem TSI-mer SHLAH-fen
phrases.note: Darf ...? asks if something is allowed. Use dürfen, not können, when you want permission. schlafen goes last.
klauen = to nick (casual for steal). die Socke is feminine, so mein becomes meine.

phrases.en: Do I have to walk him?
phrases.de: Muss ich mit ihm Gassi gehen?
phrases.ph: mus ish mit eem GA-see GAY-en
phrases.note: Muss ich ...? = Do I have to ...? – the ultimate moaning question. Gassi gehen lands at the end.
süß = sweet, and also cute. Der here is a chatty 'he' – Germans often use der/die instead of er/sie.
stinken = to stink – nearly English. For he/she/it just add -t: er stinkt.
dringend = urgently. baden = to have a bath, and muss (must) sends it to the end.
Wer = who (where is wo). brav = well-behaved – used for good dogs and good kids. ein Braver = a good one.
jemand = someone or anyone. gefüttert is the past form of füttern (to feed an animal).
wieder alone = again. schon wieder = again (and I'm fed up) – it adds a 'not again!' feel.
Runter! = Down! (short for herunter). Dog commands in German are often just one word.
One firm word, from sitzen. Not to be confused with Setz dich!, which is how you'd tell a person to sit.
her = towards the speaker; hin = away from them. So Komm her! means come over to me.
Aus! is the standard 'drop it' dog command. Normally aus means out or off, as in Licht aus (lights off).
brav = good, well-behaved. It becomes braver because Hund is a der word with no der in front.
ablecken = to lick all over; ab jumps to the end. Same root as lecker (tasty) – which is a bit gross.

phrases.de: Er liegt schon wieder auf meinem Bett.
phrases.ph: ayr leekt shohn VEE-der owf MY-nem bet
phrases.note: liegt = is lying. German often says whether something lies or stands, where English just says 'is'.

phrases.en: Can I give him a treat?
phrases.de: Darf ich ihm ein Leckerli geben?
phrases.ph: darf ish eem ine LE-ker-lee GAY-ben
phrases.note: Darf ich ...? = May I ...? – the right way to ask permission. geben (to give) goes to the end.

phrases.en: It's not my turn to walk him.
phrases.de: Ich bin nicht dran mit Gassigehen.
phrases.ph: ish bin nisht dran mit GA-see-gay-en
phrases.note: dran sein = to be your turn. das Gassigehen is Gassi gehen turned into a noun, so it's one word with a capital G.
Lass das! = Leave it! / Stop that! from lassen (to leave, let). Works on siblings as well as dogs.
In speech wohin (where to) splits: Wo ... hin? Plain wo only asks where something is.
wem = whom, the form used after mit. English can end with 'with'; German must put mit first.
Adding alles asks for the full list: 'Who all is coming?' mitkommen = to come along, so mit goes to the end.

phrases.en: What are you going to do?
phrases.note: vorhaben = to plan, so it's 'What are you lot planning?' ihr because it's about you and your friends.
losgehen = to set off, with los jumping to the end. Wann = when – don't confuse it with wenn (if/whenever).

phrases.en: What time will you be back?
phrases.note: wieder da = back again. German often uses the present for the future, so bist du here means 'will you be'.
hinkommen = to get there. hin means 'there, away from here' and lands at the end.
German has no handy word for 'lift', so it's 'Shall I drive you?' Soll ich ...? = Shall I ...?

phrases.en: Do you want me to take you?
phrases.de: Willst du, dass ich dich bringe?
phrases.ph: vilst doo, das ish dish BRING-uh
phrases.note: After dass (that) the verb goes to the end: ... dass ich dich bringe. bringen = to take someone somewhere.
abholen = to pick someone up. It stays in one piece at the end because soll is the main verb.

phrases.en: Message me when you get there.
phrases.de: Schreib mir, wenn du da bist.
phrases.ph: shripe meer, ven doo dah bist
phrases.note: Schreib mir (write to me) is used for texting too. After wenn (when), the verb bist goes to the end.

phrases.en: Let me know if your plans change.
phrases.de: Sag Bescheid, wenn sich was ändert.
phrases.ph: zahk be-SHITE, ven zish vas EN-dert
phrases.note: Bescheid sagen = to let someone know. Sag Bescheid! is everywhere in German – well worth learning.
das Handy = mobile phone. anlassen = to leave on, so an goes to the end.

phrases.en: Make sure your phone has some charge.
phrases.de: Achte darauf, dass dein Handy geladen ist.
phrases.ph: AKH-tuh da-ROWF, das dine HEN-dee ge-LAH-den ist
phrases.note: Achte darauf, dass ... = Make sure that ... geladen = charged, from laden. ist goes to the end after dass.
dabeihaben = to have on you. das Geld = money – a capitalised noun. genug sounds a bit like 'enough'.
die Jacke is the everyday word for a coat or jacket. der Mantel is a long, smart coat.
mitnehmen = to take with you. In a command it splits: Nimm ... mit!
draußen = outside. Starting with Draußen puts ist in second place, so es comes after it.
Literally 'it rains' – German has no 'is ...ing'. der Regen = rain, regnen = to rain.
zu before an adjective means too: zu spät (too late), zu kalt (too cold). Komm = come (home).
aufpassen auf = to look after. Pass auf dich auf = look after yourself – and yes, auf really appears twice.
der Spaß = fun, so Viel Spaß! is 'lots of fun'. The ß is a sharp double s.
bis = until, so it's 'until later'. Also handy: Bis dann! (see you then) and Bis gleich! (see you in a bit).
sich treffen = to meet up. ihr trefft euch = you lot meet each other – euch means 'each other' here.
fahren = to drive, but for he/she/it the a gets dots: er fährt, wer fährt.

phrases.en: Will there be an adult there?
phrases.note: ein Erwachsener = an adult, from erwachsen (grown up). dabei here means 'there with you'.
bleiben = to stay. Bleibt is the ihr command, for a whole group of friends. zusammen = together.

phrases.en: Don't go off on your own.
phrases.note: alleine (or allein) = on your own. weggehen = to go off, so weg goes right to the end.
der Schlüssel = key; Germans usually say it in the singular. It's deinen, not dein, because it's the thing you take.
rangehen = to answer the phone. anrufen = to ring someone; after wenn, anrufe goes to the end.
nach Hause = home, when you're heading there. zu Hause = at home. Mixing them up is a common GCSE slip.

phrases.en: I'll pick you up at ten.
phrases.de: Ich hol dich um zehn ab.
phrases.ph: ish hohl dish um tsayn ap
phrases.note: um + a number = at (a time): um zehn = at ten. abholen splits: hol ... ab.

phrases.en: Say hi to them from me.
phrases.note: grüßen = to greet, so it's 'greet them from me'. On a message you'd write Liebe Grüße (love from).
weggehen = to go out with friends. Darf ich asks for permission; Kann ich only asks whether you're able to.
dürfen = to be allowed. With wir it's dürfen (with dots), with ich it's darf. hingehen = to go there.
