fahren = to drive, so this is really 'Can you drive me?' mich = me, the one being driven.

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift?
phrases.note: Kannst du ...? means 'Can you ...?' – a handy pattern. fahren is to drive, so mich fahren = drive me.
abholen = to pick up (a person). After kannst, the whole verb sits at the end and doesn't split: ... mich abholen?
hinbringen = take somewhere. hin means 'there, away from here', bringen means bring. uns = us.

phrases.en: Can you pick us up later?
phrases.note: später = later. Word order tip: extra info like später goes in the middle, and abholen stays right at the end.
Darf comes from dürfen (to be allowed). meine Freundin = my (female) friend – it can also mean girlfriend. For a boy: mein Freund.

phrases.en: Can I have a friend over?
phrases.note: einladen = to invite. eine Freundin (a friend) avoids the 'girlfriend' meaning of meine Freundin. For a boy: einen Freund.
vorbeikommen = to come round or drop by. vorbei means 'past' or 'by'. sie = she; for a boy, use er.
das Abendessen is literally 'evening food' = dinner. zum is short for zu dem (to/for the).

phrases.de: Darf sie heute bei uns übernachten?
phrases.ph: darf zee HOY-tuh by uns ew-ber-NAKH-ten
phrases.note: übernachten = to stay the night (über + Nacht). bei uns means 'at ours' – no word for house needed.

phrases.en: Can I stay at her house?
phrases.note: bei ihr = at her place (bei ihm for a boy). German uses bei + person where English says 'at someone's house'.
da here means 'there', casual everyday German. Swap in bei ihr or bei ihm to say whose place.

phrases.en: What time do I have to be home?
phrases.de: Wann muss ich zu Hause sein?
phrases.ph: van mus ish tsoo HOW-zuh zine
phrases.note: zu Hause = at home; nach Hause = (going) home. muss sends the second verb, sein, to the end.

phrases.en: Do I have to come home that early?
phrases.de: Muss ich wirklich so früh nach Hause?
phrases.ph: mus ish VIRK-lish zoh frew nahkh HOW-zuh
phrases.note: Germans often drop the verb of movement: Muss ich nach Hause? already means 'Do I have to go home?'
alle anderen = everyone else. länger means 'longer', which is how German says staying later.
schreiben (write) is also the word for texting. German often uses the present tense for the future, so no 'will' needed.
Bescheid sagen is a fixed phrase meaning 'to let someone know'. Learn it as one chunk – der Bescheid rarely shows up alone.
unterwegs = on the way, or out and about. Great for texts to Mum or Dad.
losfahren = to set off (by car, bus or bike). It splits: fahren stays second and los jumps to the end.
False friend: fast means 'almost', not quick (quick is schnell). da = there.
da can mean here or there. Ich bin da is the standard way to say you've arrived.
draußen = outside. Germans say 'I'm standing outside' – steh is a casual short form of stehe.
Watch out: wo means where, and wer means who – easy to mix up because they look backwards to English.
Literally 'how long do you still need?' brauchen = to need. noch adds the 'still'.
sich beeilen = to hurry. It needs dich (yourself) with it – German says 'hurry yourself'.

phrases.en: Can I go to the cinema?
phrases.note: das Kino = cinema. ins is short for in das, used when going into somewhere.

phrases.en: I'm going to my friend's house.
phrases.note: zu + person means 'to their place'. meine changes to meiner after zu; for a boy it's zu meinem Freund.

phrases.de: Wir treffen uns in der Stadt.
phrases.ph: veer TRE-fen uns in dayr shtat
phrases.note: sich treffen = to meet up; uns means 'each other'. in der Stadt = in town.

phrases.en: Can I go to a party on Saturday?
phrases.de: Darf ich am Samstag auf eine Party gehen?
phrases.ph: darf ish am ZAMS-tahk owf EYE-nuh PAR-tee GAY-en
phrases.note: German goes auf (on) a party, not to one. am Samstag = on Saturday – am is short for an dem.
In German you 'have' your birthday: Sie hat Geburtstag. der Geburtstag = birth + day.

phrases.de: Ich bleibe heute Abend zu Hause.
phrases.ph: ish BLY-buh HOY-tuh AH-bent tsoo HOW-zuh
phrases.note: heute Abend = this evening, tonight. heute Nacht means during the night, when you'd be asleep.

phrases.en: Her mum will bring me back.
phrases.note: Ihre = her here (seine = his). zurückbringen splits: bringt stays second and zurück (back) goes to the end.

phrases.en: Can I stay a bit longer?
phrases.de: Darf ich noch ein bisschen bleiben?
phrases.ph: darf ish nokh ine BIS-shen BLY-ben
phrases.note: noch ein bisschen = a little bit more. Swap the verb to reuse it: noch ein bisschen spielen.
bis = by or until. um zehn would mean at exactly ten; bis zehn gives you until then.

phrases.en: Wait for me in the car.
phrases.note: warten auf = to wait for. English says 'for', German says auf. das Auto = car.
her means 'towards me'. Its opposite hin means 'away from me', as in Geh hin! (Go there!).
weggehen = to go away. In a command it splits: Geh first, weg at the end. Quite blunt.
mal is a little word that softens a command – like saying 'just'. Warte on its own sounds sharper.
da = there. Commands to one person often use the verb with the -st and du dropped: du wartest → Warte!
zuhören = to listen. In the command the zu splits off and goes to the end.
gucken = to look, very common at home. The mal makes it sound like 'just look at this'.
German spells it with double p. Stopp! is for stopping movement; Hör auf! is for stopping an activity.
nicht means not. Said sharply on its own, it works like 'Don't!' – for when there's no time for more.
lassen = to leave or let. Lass das! (leave that) is the everyday way to say 'Don't do that'.
liegen = to lie (be lying there). Literally 'let it lie' – leave it where it is.
hinlegen = to put down (flat). It splits: Leg ... hin! For standing things like bottles, use Stell das hin!
hergeben = hand over. her (towards me) goes to the end, so Gib das her! means 'give that here'.
bringen works just like English bring. her makes it 'to me': Bring das her!
nimm comes from nehmen (to take) – the e changes to i in the du command. Hier = here you go.
halten = to hold. Careful: Halt! on its own means Stop!, so the das mal makes it clear.
hilf comes from helfen (e changes to i). helfen takes mir, not mich – say Hilf mir, never Hilf mich.
die Vorsicht = caution. Shouted on its own it's the standard 'Watch out!' – you'll see it on signs too.
Sei is the command form of sein (to be), so Sei ...! = Be ...! vorsichtig = careful.
sich beeilen = to hurry. The dich (yourself) must stay: Beeil dich! – 'hurry yourself'.
langsam = slow. Adding -er makes 'slower', just like English: schnell → schneller.
sich beruhigen = to calm down. Ruhe means calm or quiet, and dich = yourself.
echt means real or genuine. Echt jetzt? = 'Really, now?' – casual, a bit disbelieving.
machen = to do and to make. da adds 'there' – a parent spotting something suspicious.
Past tense: hast (have) comes second and gemacht (done) goes to the very end.
warum = why. The answer usually starts with weil (because), which sends the verb to the end.
wie = how. On its own it can also mean 'Pardon?' – politer is Wie bitte?
wo = where (someone or something is). For where to, German uses wohin: Wohin gehst du?
wann = when, only in questions. Don't mix it up with wenn, which means when/if in normal sentences.
wer = who (not where!). gesagt is from sagen (to say) and goes to the end.
Literally 'how do you mean that?' meinen = to mean – it also means to think, as in Was meinst du?

phrases.de: Das hab ich dir doch schon gesagt.
phrases.ph: das hahp ish deer dokh shohn ge-ZAHKT
phrases.note: doch adds an 'I already told you!' feeling of irritation. schon = already. hab is short for habe.

phrases.de: Ich hab dich schon dreimal darum gebeten.
phrases.ph: ish hahp dish shohn DRY-mahl da-RUM ge-BAY-ten
phrases.note: bitten um = to ask for something, so darum = for it. Don't confuse with fragen, which is to ask a question.
Word order is flipped from English: jetzt (now) first, nicht (not) second.
gleich = in a moment, very soon. It also means 'the same' – context tells you which.
später = later, from spät (late). Add bis for a goodbye: Bis später! = See you later!
vielleicht = maybe. It's built from viel (much) + leicht (easy), though that doesn't help much with the meaning!
Short for Wir werden mal sehen (we'll see). The classic parent non-answer that usually means no.
Literally 'in no case'. der Fall = case. The positive version is Auf jeden Fall = definitely.
na is a filler like 'well', so Na gut = 'well, fine'. Sounds a bit reluctant.
meinetwegen = 'fine by me' or 'if you must'. It shows a parent giving in without much enthusiasm.
reichen = to be enough; reicht's is short for reicht es. The aber adds warning, not 'but'.
angucken = to look at. It splits: Guck ... an! with mich (me) in the middle.
False friend: still means quiet here, not 'still'. Quite firm – Ruhe! is even shorter.
sprich is from sprechen (to speak), e changes to i. leiser = quieter, from leise (quiet).
antworten = to answer. Like helfen, it takes mir, not mich: Antworte mir!

phrases.en: Don't talk to me like that.
phrases.note: German says 'talk like that with me' – mit mir, not zu mir. reden = to talk.
ernst = serious. Ich mein das ernst = I mean it seriously. mein is short for meine (from meinen).
klar = clear, but Klar! or Na klar! is the everyday 'Of course!' Natürlich works too but is less casual.
was = what. Blunt – fine at home, but Wie bitte? is the polite way to ask someone to repeat.
When shouted back, Germans drop the ich: Komme! = (I'm) coming!
der Moment = moment. Moment mal = hang on a sec. Moment! on its own works too.
nein = no. In casual chat you'll hear Nee or the sulky Nö – both fine at home.
Short and moany: warum = why, ich = I/me. German uses ich here, not mich.
gleich = in a moment. Ja, gleich! is the classic teen stalling answer – 'yeah, in a sec'.
boah is a teen sigh or groan, like 'ugh'. na gut = fine then.
aufhören = to stop. damit means 'with it', so this is 'stop with it!' – a bit sharper than just Hör auf!
Literally 'away there!' Blunt – fine with your sister, rude to anyone else. Politer: Kannst du mal Platz machen?
zurückgeben = to give back. It splits: Gib first, zurück (back) at the end.
German spells it Psst! or Pst! – no vowels needed. Leise! (quiet!) is the word version.
Literally 'I have to do' = I've got things to do. The adjective beschäftigt (busy) also works.
Mach schon! = get on with it! machen = do, schon adds impatience. Rude-ish but normal at home.
schauen = to look, used a lot in southern Germany. mal turns it into 'have a look!'
abhauen = to clear off. Very blunt – fine with your sister, but don't say it to a parent or a teacher.
egal = all the same. Mir egal = '(It's) all the same to me' – the classic teen shrug.
nicht goes after the word it cancels: Ich nicht = not me. Compare Jetzt nicht = not now.
war is the past of sein (to be); war's is short for war es. Literally 'I wasn't it!'
wartet is the ihr form, for when the whole family is leaving. To just one person: Warte auf mich!
die Ruhe = peace and quiet. Literally 'leave me in peace'. Moody but not rude.
Literally 'how goes it to you?' geht's = geht es. Answer: Gut, danke! or Geht so (so-so).
los here means 'going on'. Was ist los? = what's up / what's the matter.
weißt comes from wissen (to know a fact). Note the ß – it sounds like ss.
war's = war es (was it). wie = how. Perfect after school, a party or a match.
erzählen = to tell (a story or news). mal makes it friendly: 'go on, tell me'.
wirklich = really. Casual swap: Echt? – you'll hear that from teens all the time.
ja here isn't 'yes' – it adds excitement, like 'that's really great!'
Same as English, but nein has the German ei sound – like English 'nine'.
Literally 'what have you got?' – a kind way to ask what's wrong. denn makes it sound caring.
wer = who, war = was. Useful after a phone call or the doorbell.
denken = to think. For 'what do you think about it?' add dazu: Was denkst du dazu?
es gibt = there is, so this is literally 'that doesn't exist!' – pure disbelief.
gehen + another verb at the end = go and do something: Ich geh arbeiten = I'm off to work.
um + number = at that time: um sechs = at six. zurück = back.
Ich hab dich lieb is for family and friends. Ich liebe dich is mostly romantic.
gerade = right now, at the moment. German has no '-ing' form, so this word does the job.
der Tag = day, so it's dein (your) with no ending. war = was.
Literally 'is it going well for you?' dir = to you. Answer: Ja, alles gut.
müde = tired. The ü is said with rounded lips, like saying 'ee' while whistling.
was für ein = what a. Reuse it: Was für ein Chaos! = What a mess!
wieder = again, so 'I'm here again' – the standard shout when you walk in the door.
die Sorge = worry. Literally 'make yourself no worries'. keine = no/not any.
in Ordnung = okay, all right (literally 'in order'). die Ordnung – capital O as it's a noun.
stolz = proud. German says proud on you: stolz auf + dich.

phrases.en: Did you have a good time?
phrases.note: Spaß haben = to have fun. Hattest is the simple past of haben (to have), which Germans use a lot in speech.
Papa is what German kids call their dad. When talking about him to a teacher you might say mein Vater.
Mama is the everyday word. die Mutter is more formal, e.g. meine Mutter when talking about her to someone else.
Was? is blunt, just like 'What?' in English. Wie bitte? is the polite way to ask someone to repeat something.
machen means both 'do' and 'make'. German has no separate '-ing' form, so Was machst du? covers 'What are you doing?'.
Wo = where. Don't mix it up with wer, which means 'who'. bist is 'are' when talking to one person (du).
Wohin = where to. German uses wo for 'at which place' and wohin for 'to which place'. Wo gehst du hin? also works.
No 'the' or 'my' is needed: Mama works like a name here. In speech Wo ist often blurs into Wo is.
Wo ist ...? = Where is ...? Swap in anything you've lost: Wo ist mein Handy? Wo ist meine Jacke?
You could also ask Wo ist der Hund? der Hund (the dog) has a capital H because every German noun does.
Literally 'How late is it?' — the standard way to ask the time. Wie viel Uhr ist es? means the same.
Literally 'Which day is today?'. welcher = which, and its ending changes with the noun: welcher Tag, welche Woche.
losfahren = to set off (in a car). It splits: fahren sits second and los jumps to the very end.
Verb second: when a question word like Was starts the sentence, the verb machen comes straight after it.
irgendwohin = (to) anywhere. irgend- means 'some-/any-': irgendwas (something), irgendwer (someone).
German often drops the 'go' verb after können when it's obvious. los here means 'off', so it's 'Can we be off now?'.
fertig can mean 'ready' or 'finished', so Bist du fertig? depends on context. bereit is a more formal 'ready'.

phrases.en: How long are you going to be?
phrases.note: brauchen normally means 'to need', but with time it means 'to take'. noch = still, so 'how much longer do you need?'.

phrases.de: Komm mal her und guck dir das an!
phrases.ph: kom mahl hayr unt guk deer das an
phrases.note: her means 'towards me', so Komm her! = Come here! The little word mal makes a command sound casual and friendly.
gucken is the everyday word for 'look' (schauen in the south). Guck mal! is what you'd say while pointing at something.
aufpassen = to pay attention. In a command the auf splits off to the end. Before showing off a trick it means 'Watch this!'
sich etwas anhören = to listen to something. The an jumps to the end, and dir (to yourself) is needed in German.
raten = to guess. Rate mal! is how Germans start telling news, just like 'Guess what!'
After was in the middle of a sentence, the verb goes to the end: was passiert ist. German always puts a comma before it.

phrases.de: Du errätst nie, was passiert ist.
phrases.ph: doo er-RAYTST nee, vas pa-SEERT ist
phrases.note: erraten = to guess correctly; nie = never. The du form gains an umlaut: ich errate, but du errätst.
lustig = funny (the ha-ha kind). It has nothing to do with the English word 'lust'.
komisch looks like 'comic', but usually means weird or strange. seltsam is another word for weird.
nerven = to annoy, to get on your nerves. Das nervt! is exactly what a German teenager would say.
eklig = disgusting, gross. It's often paired with Igitt!, the German 'Eww!'.
peinlich = embarrassing. Wie peinlich! (How embarrassing!) is a favourite teen reaction to parents.
unfair is borrowed from English. Das ist nicht fair also works; gerecht (fair, just) is the more formal word.
Literally '(It) is all the same to me'. The Das at the start gets dropped in speech. Sounds rude if said with attitude.
weiß comes from wissen (to know a fact). The letter ß is just another way of writing 'ss'. Keine Ahnung = No idea.
vielleicht = maybe. It also softens a request: Kannst du mir vielleicht helfen? = Could you maybe help me?
wahrscheinlich = probably. It's built from wahr (true) and scheinen (to seem) — 'seeming true'.
Na gut = Fine, with a reluctant tone. na is a filler word like 'well' — you'll hear it all the time.
Okay is used in German just as in English. Alternatives: In Ordnung (all right) or Alles klar (got it).
Egal on its own is the dismissive teen 'Whatever.' Said with a shrug, it sounds rude to adults.
echt = real, genuine. Echt jetzt? is the casual 'Seriously?'. Im Ernst? is a slightly less slangy option.
wirklich = really. It works alone as a question or to boost a word: wirklich gut = really good.
Auf keinen Fall! = No way! when refusing something. For amazed disbelief, Germans say Echt? or Krass! instead.
klar literally means 'clear', so Na klar = obviously, of course. Logisch! is a cheeky teen alternative.
genau = exactly. Germans use it constantly to agree with someone, so you'll hear it everywhere.
No 'it' needed: Ich weiß! = I know! Add doch — Ich weiß doch! — to sound extra annoyed.
aufhören = to stop doing something, and the auf splits off to the end. Stopp! is used for stopping movement.
Literally 'Leave me in peace'. die Ruhe = peace and quiet — capitalised because it's a noun.
weggehen = to go away; in a command weg jumps to the end. Blunt — fine with your sister, rude to anyone else.
Du nervst comes from nerven (to annoy). -st is the ending for du on almost every verb: du gehst, du machst.
total = totally, a hugely common booster in casual German. Du bist so nervig! also works (nervig = annoying).
Danke = thanks. Danke schön or Vielen Dank sound warmer. German keeps the comma before Mama too.

phrases.de: Tut mir leid, das wollte ich nicht.
phrases.ph: toot meer lite, das VOL-tuh ish nisht
phrases.note: Tut mir leid = I'm sorry. das wollte ich nicht is literally 'that I didn't want' — das goes first for emphasis.
Hab dich lieb is how family members say 'Love you'. Ich liebe dich is for romantic love, so skip it with parents.
Literally 'To me it is boring'. Don't say Ich bin langweilig — that means 'I am boring'!
cool is borrowed from English and used the same way. Voll cool = really cool; voll (full) is a common teen booster.
keine Sorge = no worry (die Sorge = worry). Schon gut = It's fine, often said when accepting an apology.
was here is short for etwas (something). Kann ich ...? = Can I ...? is a pattern you can reuse everywhere.
der Spaß = fun, or a joke. Literally '(That) was only fun'. Ich mache nur Spaß (I'm only joking) also works.
zu Hause = at home, but nach Hause = (to) home: Ich gehe nach Hause. German uses different words for 'at' and 'to'.
Ich auch = me too. German uses ich (I), not mich (me), so it's literally 'I also'.
Literally 'Everything OK?'. Alles in Ordnung? is the slightly more formal version of the same question.
Was ist los? = What's wrong? / What's going on? Here los has nothing to do with 'lost'.
wirken = to seem. bedrückt = down, upset — it comes from drücken (to press), like feeling weighed down.
sich fühlen = to feel. The dich (yourself) is needed: German says 'Do you feel yourself not well?'.
das Pflaster = plaster. Brauchst du ...? = Do you need ...? — swap in anything: Brauchst du Hilfe?
wehtun = to hurt, and it splits: tut ... weh. Same pattern for body parts: Mir tut das Knie weh = My knee hurts.

phrases.en: Do you want to talk about it?
phrases.note: darüber = about it (da + über). After Willst du, the second verb (reden, to talk) goes to the end.
Literally 'Make yourself no worries'. keine (no, not any) is used before nouns, where English says 'don't'.

phrases.en: Try not to stress about your exams.
phrases.de: Mach dir wegen der Prüfungen nicht so viel Stress.
phrases.ph: makh deer VAY-gen dayr PREW-fung-en nisht zoh feel shtres
phrases.note: wegen = because of. die Prüfung = exam; for a normal school test you'll hear Klassenarbeit or Test.
Du solltest ... = You should ... The second verb goes to the end. sich ausruhen = to rest.
aussehen = to look (how something appears). It splits, and aus goes to the end: Du siehst müde aus.
Literally 'Does it go better for you?' — the classic German way to ask about health. besser = better.

phrases.de: Du bist heute aber schlecht gelaunt!
phrases.ph: doo bist HOY-tuh AH-ber shlesht ge-LOWNT
phrases.note: aber here isn't 'but' — it adds surprise, like 'really'. schlecht gelaunt = in a bad mood, grumpy.
Literally 'Head up!'. der Kopf = head. A short, friendly way to tell someone to cheer up.
Sei is the command form of sein (to be): Sei leise! Sei nett! Stell dich nicht so an! is a very German alternative.
Nimm comes from nehmen (to take). The e changes to i in the du command: nehmen becomes Nimm!

phrases.en: Do you need to see the doctor?
phrases.note: zum = zu dem (to the). der Arzt = doctor; a female doctor is die Ärztin. The 'go' verb is left out, as often in German.

phrases.de: Ist in der Schule was passiert?
phrases.ph: ist in dayr SHOO-luh vas pa-SEERT
phrases.note: passieren = to happen. In the past it uses ist, not hat: ist passiert. in der Schule = at school.

phrases.en: Go and lie down for a bit.
phrases.note: sich hinlegen = to lie down. hin splits off to the end, and dich (yourself) is needed. ein bisschen = a bit.
glühen = to glow, like hot coals. The ja here doesn't mean 'yes' — it shows surprise.
getrunken is the past form of trinken (to drink). With hast, it goes to the very end of the sentence.

phrases.en: It's not the end of the world.
phrases.de: Davon geht die Welt nicht unter.
phrases.ph: da-FON gayt dee velt nisht UN-ter
phrases.note: A fixed saying: literally 'The world won't go under from that'. untergehen = to sink, and unter splits to the end.
Literally 'To me it goes not well'. The sentence starts with mir (to me), not ich. geht's = geht es.
Kopfschmerzen = Kopf (head) + Schmerzen (pains). German builds words like Lego, and it's always plural here.
der Bauch = tummy, belly. Mir tut der Bauch weh (My tummy hurts) is another common way to say it.
der Hals means both throat and neck, so Halsschmerzen can be either — context makes it clear.

phrases.en: I think I've got a temperature.
phrases.note: das Fieber = temperature, fever. Ich glaube, ... = I think ... — note the comma German needs after it.

phrases.de: Ich mache mir Sorgen wegen der Prüfungen.
phrases.ph: ish MA-khuh meer ZOR-gen VAY-gen dayr PREW-fung-en
phrases.note: sich Sorgen machen = to worry, literally 'to make yourself worries'. wegen = because of, about.
Literally 'The exams stress me totally'. stressen is a German verb borrowed from English. Ich bin gestresst also works.
die Umarmung = hug, from umarmen (to hug): um (around) + Arm. A cosier option is Drück mich mal!
Literally 'I have my nose full'. die Nase = nose. It's the everyday German way to say you're fed up.
Use Mir geht's gut for 'I'm fine'. Ich bin gut sounds odd — it suggests you're good at something.
Lass comes from lassen (to let, to leave). Add doch for extra frustration: Lass mich doch in Ruhe!
niemand = nobody. verstehen (to understand) never splits, because ver- always stays stuck to the verb.
schlecht normally means 'bad', but Mir ist schlecht specifically means 'I feel sick'. Ich bin schlecht = I'm bad!
tierisch literally means 'animal-like', but in slang it means massive or really bad: tierischen Hunger, tierisch nervig.
die Regel = period (it also means 'rule'). Regelschmerzen = period pains. Ich habe meine Tage is a common way to say you're on your period.
gestresst comes from English 'stressed' but gets the German ge- at the start and ends in -sst.
Stretch the so for effect: Mir ist sooo langweilig! mir means 'to me' — German says 'to me it is boring'.
die Laune = mood. schlechte Laune haben = to be in a bad mood; gute Laune = a good mood.
False friend: will comes from wollen (to want), so Ich will = I want, not 'I will'. nur = only, just.
verhungern = to starve, from der Hunger. Germans exaggerate with it exactly like 'I'm starving!'
die Lust = the wish to do something, so keine Lust = don't feel like it. It's not the same as English 'lust'!

phrases.en: It's been the worst day ever.
phrases.de: Das war der schlimmste Tag meines Lebens.
phrases.ph: das vahr dayr SHLIMS-tuh tahk MY-nes LAY-bens
phrases.note: meines Lebens = of my life. schlimmste = worst, from schlimm (bad). German says 'of my life' where English says 'ever'.
fertig usually means ready or finished, but total fertig = shattered, completely worn out.
übertreiben = to exaggerate. Here über- stays attached and doesn't split. nicht comes after the verb.

phrases.en: I don't want to talk about it.
phrases.note: Word order: will comes second and reden (to talk) goes to the end, with nicht darüber in between.

phrases.en: I think I'm getting a cold.
phrases.de: Ich glaube, ich bekomme eine Erkältung.
phrases.ph: ish GLOW-buh, ish be-KO-muh EYE-nuh er-KEL-tung
phrases.note: False friend: bekommen = to get, never 'become'. die Erkältung = a cold.
stolz auf = proud of. German uses auf (literally 'on') where English uses 'of'.
aufgeben = to give up. In a command, auf goes to the end: Gib nicht auf! Gib comes from geben (to give).
schaffen = to manage, to pull something off. Du schaffst das! is the go-to German encouragement.
das Glück means both luck and happiness. Before an exam, Germans also say Toi, toi, toi!
super is used just like 'great'. sieht ... aus comes from aussehen (to look), with aus split off to the end.
fürs = für das. Helfen has a capital here because the verb is being used as a noun: 'the helping'.
ganz doll = ever so much — informal and warm. A family phrase; Ich liebe dich is kept for romantic love.
hübsch = pretty, lovely — usually said to girls. To a boy, Du siehst gut aus (You look good) sounds more natural.
Literally 'Further like this!'. Short and punchy — teachers write it on good work too.

phrases.en: It doesn't matter if you get it wrong.
phrases.de: Es ist nicht schlimm, wenn du etwas falsch machst.
phrases.ph: es ist nisht shlim, ven doo ET-vas falsh makhst
phrases.note: After wenn (if, when), the verb goes to the end: wenn du etwas falsch machst. falsch = wrong.
Literally 'Just give your best'. das Beste is used as a noun here, so it's capitalised. einfach = just (also 'simple').
können means 'can' but also 'know how to do'. richtig usually means 'correct', but here it means 'really'.
der Glückwunsch = good wish (Glück + Wunsch). Also for birthdays: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!
lieb = kind, sweet, used about people and pets. Das ist lieb von dir = That's kind of you.
gemacht is the past form of machen, so it's literally 'well made'. Super gemacht! is even warmer.

phrases.en: I knew you could do it.
phrases.de: Ich wusste, dass du es schaffst.
phrases.ph: ish VUS-tuh, das doo es shafst
phrases.note: After dass (that), the verb goes to the end: dass du es schaffst. wusste = knew, from wissen.
die Note = mark, grade. German school marks run from 1 (best) to 6 (worst), so a 1 is what you want!
sich anstrengen = to make an effort. In the past the ge- goes in the middle of split verbs: an-ge-strengt.
die Klasse also means class or year group, but said on its own it's praise. Spitze! means much the same.
klappen means 'to work out' – very common: Hat's geklappt? = Did it work? The 's is short for es.
Hab ich ...? is chatty for Habe ich ...? Past events use haben + a past form (gemacht, from machen), which goes to the end.
schaffen = to manage, to pull something off. Ich hab's geschafft! is the go-to cheer after finishing something hard.
To Mum it's die Beste; to Dad it's der Beste. The ending changes with who you're praising.
Note is the German for a school mark (die Note). It can also mean a musical note, like in English.
gut in etwas sein = to be good at something. Here in + das becomes darin (at it). Ich bin gut in Mathe = I'm good at maths.
Danke is the everyday thank you. Mama and Papa are what German teens actually call their parents – not Mutter or Vater.
Short for Das hab ich doch gesagt! The little word doch adds an 'I was right, wasn't I?' feeling.

phrases.de: Ich bin so stolz auf mich.
phrases.ph: ish bin zoh shtolts owf mish
phrases.note: stolz auf = proud of. German uses auf (literally 'on'), not von. Ich bin stolz auf dich = I'm proud of you.
krass is teen slang for 'amazing' or 'extreme' – it can be good or bad depending on tone. ja just adds surprise.
Gut gemacht = literally 'well done', the same as English. Easy to reuse for anyone: Gut gemacht, Monty!
schlecht means bad (not 'slight'). Nicht schlecht! works just like English – often it really means 'pretty good'.
hinkriegen is chatty for 'to manage' or 'pull off'. voll in teen speak means 'totally', not 'full'.
German grades run 1 to 6, and eine Eins (a one) is the best. Careful: a Sechs is a fail, not a good mark!
bestanden comes from bestehen = to pass (a test). Don't use passen – that means 'to fit' or 'to suit'.
Germans use cool just like English. Wie ... ist das denn! is a handy pattern for excitement: Wie geil ist das denn! is more slangy.
Sag! is the du command of sagen (to say): just drop the -en. bitte means please, and also 'you're welcome'.
Sag danke is the same pattern as Sag bitte. Some parents say Bedank dich! (thank them), from sich bedanken.
German parents ask Wie sagt man? – literally 'How does one say?'. man means 'one' or 'people', not 'man' (that's Mann).
Gern geschehen = literally 'gladly happened'. For a shorter reply, just say Bitte! or Gerne!
Kein means 'no' before a noun: kein Problem, keine Ahnung (no idea). Use nicht for verbs and adjectives instead.
Gesundheit literally means 'health'. It's what everyone says after a sneeze – the English borrowed it too.
Entschuldigung works for 'excuse me' and 'sorry'. It's a long one: break it up as Ent-schul-di-gung.
After bevor (before) the verb goes to the end: bevor du reinkommst. reinkommen = to come in.
höflich = polite, and un- flips it: unhöflich = impolite. Same trick as English: unfair, unfreundlich.
Schatz literally means 'treasure' and is the classic German pet name for a child or partner.
unterbrechen = to interrupt. The du command changes the vowel: brechen → brich. nicht goes at the end.
sich entschuldigen bei = to apologise to. After bei, dein becomes deinem (der Bruder). For a sister: bei deiner Schwester.

phrases.en: Say it like you mean it.
phrases.de: Sag es so, als ob du es ernst meinst.
phrases.ph: zahk es zoh, als op doo es ernst mynst
phrases.note: etwas ernst meinen = to mean something seriously. After als ob (as if) the verb goes to the end.

phrases.en: Don't talk with your mouth full.
phrases.note: Germans say 'with full mouth' – no 'your'. sprechen changes to sprich in a du command.

phrases.en: Don't speak to me like that.
phrases.note: German says 'talk like that WITH me' – mit mir, not zu mir. reden is a chattier word for sprechen.
aufpassen auf = to watch out for. The auf from aufpassen jumps to the end, so auf appears twice: Pass auf deinen Ton auf.
Oma = grandma, Opa = grandpa. Families use them like names, so there's no 'your' or 'the': Sag Oma Hallo.
Manieren = manners (always plural). wo bleiben literally means 'where are they staying' – a set phrase for 'where's your ...?'
Bitte is a multi-tool: please, you're welcome, and Bitte? for 'pardon?' when you didn't hear.
Danke is the everyday word. Danke schön is a bit warmer and politer.
Vielen Dank literally means 'many thanks'. Danke sehr and Danke schön mean much the same.
Tut mir leid = literally 'it does me sorrow'. Germans often use the English 'Sorry!' too for small slips.

phrases.en: Excuse me, can I get past?
phrases.note: vorbei = past. German can drop the verb: darf ich vorbei? means 'may I (go) past?'. mal makes it softer.
fürs is short for für das. das Essen means food or the meal – whatever time of day it is.
Family members say Ich hab dich lieb. Ich liebe dich is stronger and mostly for boyfriends and girlfriends.
Short and natural: Ich dich auch = 'Me you too'. German skips the repeated verb, just like 'Love you too'.
Germans use Stress too. Kein Stress is a relaxed teen way to say 'no worries' or 'don't stress'.
Adding okay? at the end makes the apology sound a bit grudging – just like in English. Germans say okay all the time.
doch here means 'I already did, so stop going on'. entschuldigt is the past form of sich entschuldigen (to apologise).

phrases.en: Sorry, can I just say something?
phrases.de: Sorry, darf ich mal kurz was sagen?
phrases.ph: SO-ree, darf ish mahl kurts vas ZAH-gen
phrases.note: mal kurz = 'just quickly' – it makes a request sound small and polite. was is chatty for etwas (something).
anklopfen = to knock. In a command it splits: Klopf ... an! erst mal means 'first of all'.

phrases.en: Sorry, I didn't do it on purpose.
phrases.de: Tut mir leid, das war keine Absicht.
phrases.ph: toot meer lite, das vahr KYE-nuh AP-zisht
phrases.note: die Absicht = intention. Das war keine Absicht = 'that was no intention' – the usual way to say 'not on purpose'.
unterbrochen is the past form of unterbrechen. Unlike many verbs it has no ge- at the start, because unter- here doesn't split off.
Fahren (driving) is capitalised here because it's used as a noun: fürs Fahren = for the driving.

phrases.en: Can I leave the table, please?
phrases.note: German kids ask 'May I stand up?' – aufstehen. Use darf ich (may I) for permission; kann ich is more 'am I able'.

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.note: Kannst du ...? = Can you ...?, with the other verb at the end. helfen takes mir (to me), not mich.

phrases.de: Hilf mir, die Einkäufe zu tragen.
phrases.ph: hilf meer, dee INE-koy-fuh tsoo TRAH-gen
phrases.note: die Einkäufe = the shopping (the bags of stuff). helfen becomes hilf in a du command.

phrases.de: Kannst du mir die Tür aufhalten?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer dee tewr OWF-hal-ten
phrases.note: aufhalten = to hold open (auf = open). Not the same as halten (to hold) – that alone would sound like gripping the door.
aufmachen = to open – when the doorbell goes, that's all you need to say. auf means open, zu means shut.
brauchen = to need. die Hilfe = help. The verb comes first to make a yes/no question: Brauchst du ...?
Soll ich ...? = Shall I ...? Great for offers: Soll ich das machen? helfen takes dir, not dich.
Lass mich! = Let me! The rest (do it) is understood. Careful: Lass mich in Ruhe! means 'Leave me alone!'
her means 'towards me' and hin means 'away from me'. Gib her! = give it (over) here.
zeigen = to show. Zeig mal! is the natural short version; mal just softens a command.
holen = to fetch or get. It's the go-to verb for 'go and get': Hol Monty rein! = Get Monty in!
German just uses geben (give) where English says 'pass'. At the table: Gib mir mal das Salz.
los on its own means 'loose' or 'going on'. Was ist los? = What's up? / What's wrong?
die Brille = glasses – it's one singular word in German, so it's meine Brille ist weg, not 'are'.
der Schlüssel = key. The plural is the same word, so 'meine' is the only clue it's more than one.
nachschauen = to look up / check. Also nachgucken or googeln – Germans happily say Kannst du das googeln?
suchen = to look for. finden = to find. Germans say 'help me look for it', since you can't promise to find it.

phrases.en: Can you set this up for me?
phrases.note: einrichten = to set up (a phone, an app). The ein- is a separable bit: Richte das ein! in a command.

phrases.en: I could do with some help here.
phrases.de: Ich könnte hier ein bisschen Hilfe gebrauchen.
phrases.ph: ish KURN-tuh heer ine BIS-shen HIL-fuh ge-BROW-khen
phrases.note: könnte = could. gebrauchen = to make use of. Ein bisschen = a bit – a polite hint rather than an order.
helfen always takes mir/dir (to me/to you), never mich/dich. Kannst du mir helfen? is a phrase worth learning by heart.

phrases.en: Can you help me with this?
phrases.note: dabei = with it (bei + das). German often squeezes 'with this' into one word like dabei, damit or davon.

phrases.en: Can you do this for me?
phrases.de: Kannst du das für mich machen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo das fewr mish MA-khen
phrases.note: für = for, and it's always followed by mich/dich (not mir/dir). machen = to do or make.
aufmachen = to open, zumachen = to close. Both are chatty and used for jars, doors, bags – anything.
rankommen = to reach (literally 'come at'). It splits: Kommst du da ran? – the ran jumps to the end.
reparieren = to repair. Most -ieren verbs look like English: reparieren, telefonieren, probieren.

phrases.de: Kannst du dir das mal ansehen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo deer das mahl AN-zay-en
phrases.note: sich etwas ansehen = to have a look at something. The dir means 'for yourself' – odd in English but normal in German.
kontrollieren = to check, not 'to control' – a false friend. For homework you can also say durchsehen.
Wie geht das? = literally 'How does that go?'. Same verb as Wie geht's? (How are you?).
bedeuten = to mean. Don't use meinen here – that's 'to mean' as in 'think': Was meinst du? = What do you think?
hinkommen = to go (somewhere) when tidying. Germans say 'where does this come to?' – wo ... hin = where to.
When es (it) and mir (me) meet, es comes first: es mir zeigen. zeigen = to show.
Germans usually drop 'here' and add mal: Kannst du mal kommen? Shouting from upstairs: Mama, komm mal!
halten = to hold. It also means 'to stop' – a bus hält an der Haltestelle (stops at the bus stop).
tragen = to carry, and also to wear clothes: Ich trage einen Hoodie.

phrases.en: Can you get this for me?
phrases.note: holen = to fetch. mir here means 'for me' – German often uses mir where English needs 'for me'.
Germans often just use the plain verb instead of 'can you': Findest du es? = Can you find it?
gesehen is the past form of sehen (to see). The past form always goes to the end of the sentence.

phrases.en: Can you give me a hand?
phrases.note: mit anfassen = to lend a hand (literally 'grab hold with me'). Perfect for lifting or carrying things.
klemmen = to be stuck or jammed. Germans say 'it jams' as a verb: Die Tür klemmt = The door's stuck.
kaputt = broken. English 'kaput' comes from it. It works for phones, toys, anything.
funktionieren = to work (for machines). For people 'work' is arbeiten. Chattier: Das geht nicht.
hinkriegen = to manage. Ich krieg das nicht hin = I can't get it to work. kriegen is chatty for bekommen.

phrases.de: Kannst du mir das noch mal erklären?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer das nokh mahl er-KLAY-ren
phrases.note: noch mal = once more / again. erklären = to explain. Very useful at school, too.
wehtun = to hurt. German says 'I have done myself pain': Ich hab mir wehgetan. Aua! = Ow!

phrases.de: Ich hab mich in den Finger geschnitten.
phrases.ph: ish hahp mish in dayn FING-er ge-SHNI-ten
phrases.note: German says 'I've cut myself into the finger' – no 'my'. der Finger is the same word as in English.
leihen = to lend or borrow. deins = yours (for a das word); it's deinen for a der word, deine for a die word.

phrases.en: I don't know how it works.
phrases.de: Ich weiß nicht, wie das geht.
phrases.ph: ish vice nisht, vee das gayt
phrases.note: After wie (how) in the middle of a sentence, the verb moves to the end: wie das geht. weiß uses the ß letter.
schwer means heavy and also difficult: Die Klassenarbeit war schwer. zu = too.
The same saying exists in German. der Baum becomes Bäume in the plural, and Bäumen after auf here.

phrases.en: What do you need it for?
phrases.note: Wofür? = What for? (wo + für). The question word comes first and the verb comes second.
teuer = expensive, billig = cheap. Same pattern as zu schwer, zu laut: zu means too.
Wie viel kostet ...? = How much is ...? In a shop it's the phrase you need. Wie viel is written as two words.

phrases.de: Bezahl das von deinem eigenen Geld.
phrases.ph: be-TSAHL das fon DYE-nem EYE-ge-nen gelt
phrases.note: eigen = own. bezahlen = to pay for. von deinem Geld = out of your money (das Geld → deinem after von).

phrases.en: You've already spent your pocket money.
phrases.de: Du hast dein Taschengeld schon ausgegeben.
phrases.ph: doo hast dine TA-shen-gelt shohn OWS-ge-gay-ben
phrases.note: das Taschengeld = pocket money (Tasche = pocket + Geld). ausgeben = to spend money; ausgegeben is its past form.

phrases.de: Ich geb dir die Hälfte dazu.
phrases.ph: ish gayp deer dee HELF-tuh da-TSOO
phrases.note: die Hälfte = half. dazugeben = to chip in (give towards). German often uses the present tense for 'I'll'.

phrases.en: Put it on your birthday list.
phrases.note: sich etwas wünschen = to wish for something. zum Geburtstag = for your birthday – no 'your' needed.
Putting Das first adds stress, like 'THAT we're not buying'. The verb still comes second: Das kaufen wir.
das Kleingeld = change, coins (literally 'small money'). Don't use Wechsel – that means an exchange.
rausschmeißen = to throw out, so rausgeschmissenes Geld is 'thrown-away money'. Another way to say it: Geldverschwendung.
schicken = to send, geschickt is its past form. Careful: geschickt on its own can also mean 'skilful'.
brauchen = to need. Starting with das puts the focus on the thing: 'That, you don't need.'

phrases.en: What happened to your birthday money?
phrases.de: Was ist mit deinem Geburtstagsgeld passiert?
phrases.ph: vas ist mit DYE-nem ge-BOORTS-tahks-gelt pa-SEERT
phrases.note: Geburtstagsgeld = birthday money: German glues nouns together, and the last one (Geld) decides it's das.
sparen = to save (money). Your savings are Ersparnisse; a piggy bank is ein Sparschwein.

phrases.en: Do I look like a bank?
phrases.de: Seh ich aus wie eine Bank?
phrases.ph: zay ish ows vee EYE-nuh bank
phrases.note: aussehen wie = to look like; it splits: Seh ich aus wie ...? Careful: die Bank also means a bench!
der Monat = month, so dieser changes to diesen for 'this month' as a time. nicht goes after it.

phrases.en: You'll have to pay me back.
phrases.note: zurückzahlen = to pay back (zurück = back). With musst, the second verb stays whole at the end.
warten auf = to wait for – German uses auf, not für. der Schlussverkauf = the end-of-season sale.

phrases.en: Do you think I'm made of money?
phrases.note: Krösus was a super-rich ancient king – Germans use his name to mean a millionaire. Also: Ich bin doch kein Goldesel!

phrases.de: Kann ich ein bisschen Geld haben?
phrases.ph: kan ish ine BIS-shen gelt HAH-ben
phrases.note: ein bisschen = a bit / some. das Geld = money, always singular in German.

phrases.en: Can you send me some money?
phrases.note: German often drops 'some': Kannst du mir Geld schicken? Online it's also überweisen (to transfer).
German flips it: 'Can you lend me money?' leihen covers both lend and borrow; the mir shows who gets it.
zurückzahlen splits in a normal sentence: Ich zahl's dir zurück – zurück jumps to the end.
Asking permission? Use darf ich (may I). Kann ich das kaufen? can sound like 'Am I able to buy this?'

phrases.en: Can you buy this for me?
phrases.note: A short, cheeky way to ask: Kaufst du mir das? = literally 'Will you buy me that?' No 'for' needed thanks to mir.
bestellen = to order (online or food). was is chatty for etwas (something).
die Karte = card (bank card, also ticket or map). benutzen = to use.
Wie viel = how much, and kostet comes from kosten (to cost). Reuse it in any shop: Wie viel kostet ...? plus the thing.
Pfund = pound (money and weight). After a number it doesn't add a plural ending: fünf Pfund, zehn Pfund.
im Angebot = on offer. On shop signs you'll also see reduziert (reduced) and Sale.
brauchen = to need. Ich brauche ... is a handy pattern: Ich brauche Geld, Ich brauche neue Schuhe.
Jeder = everyone, but it takes a singular verb: jeder hat, not jeder haben. The classic teen argument for buying something.
shoppen is borrowed from English and means fun shopping (clothes etc.). einkaufen is the everyday word, often for food.

phrases.de: Können wir in die Stadt fahren?
phrases.ph: KUR-nen veer in dee shtat FAH-ren
phrases.note: in die Stadt = into town. die Stadt means both town and city, and Germans use it for the town centre.

phrases.en: Can you take me to the shops?
phrases.de: Kannst du mich zu den Geschäften fahren?
phrases.ph: kanst doo mish tsoo dayn ge-SHEF-ten FAH-ren
phrases.note: fahren can mean to drive someone: Kannst du mich ... fahren? = Can you drive me ...? das Geschäft = shop, plural Geschäfte.

phrases.en: I don't have any money left.
phrases.note: kein ... mehr = none left, no more. It works for anything: Ich habe keine Zeit mehr = I've got no time left.

phrases.en: Can I have my pocket money?
phrases.note: Taschengeld = Tasche (pocket) + Geld (money). It's das Taschengeld, so you say mein, not meine.
sparen = to save money. gerade means right now, giving the -ing feel. Ich spare auf ein neues Handy = I'm saving for a new phone.
Here zu means too, not to. teuer = expensive; the opposite is billig or günstig.
billig = cheap, but it can sound cheap-and-nasty. günstig is the positive good-value word. echt = really, very casual.

phrases.en: I want to buy her a present.
phrases.de: Ich will ihr ein Geschenk kaufen.
phrases.ph: ish vil eer ine ge-SHENK KOW-fen
phrases.note: ihr here means for her. After will, the second verb kaufen jumps to the very end of the sentence.

phrases.en: Can I use my birthday money?
phrases.note: Geburtstagsgeld glues Geburtstag (birthday) + Geld (money). The last part decides the gender: das Geld, so das Geburtstagsgeld.
ausgeben = to spend money. In the past form the ge slots in between: aus-ge-geben. Don't mix up with verbringen (spend time).

phrases.en: Can you lend me ten pounds?
phrases.de: Kannst du mir zehn Pfund leihen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer tsayn pfunt LYE-en
phrases.note: leihen = to lend (or borrow). mir = to me. Kannst du mir ...? is the go-to pattern for asking a favour.
sich lohnen = to be worth it. The sich is part of the phrase, so keep it. Das lohnt sich nicht = it's not worth it.
das Wechselgeld = change (money back), from wechseln (to swap). behalten = to keep. Darf ich? is the polite May I?
Parents often bark a whole verb as a command: Anschnallen! = Belt up! The full version is Schnall dich an!

phrases.de: Hör auf, gegen den Sitz zu treten!
phrases.ph: hur owf, GAY-gen dayn zits tsoo TRAY-ten
phrases.note: Hör auf, ... zu + verb = Stop ...ing. The action goes last with zu in front: zu treten (to kick).
weglegen = to put away. In a command it splits: Leg ... weg! Handy is the German word for mobile phone.
fast = almost. False friend alert: it never means quick, which is schnell.
dauern = to take (time). nicht mehr lange = not much longer. A parent's favourite line on any long drive.

phrases.en: Go to the toilet before we leave.
phrases.de: Geh noch mal auf die Toilette, bevor wir losfahren.
phrases.ph: gay nokh mahl owf dee toy-LE-tuh, be-FOR veer LOHS-fah-ren
phrases.note: After bevor (before) the verb goes to the end: bevor wir losfahren. losfahren = to set off.
Seid is the command of sein (to be) for two or more people. To just one person it's Sei nicht so laut!
versuchen = to try. sich konzentrieren always takes a self-word, so with ich it becomes mich zu konzentrieren.
ablenken = to distract. In a command it splits: Lenk ... ab! and nicht sits just before the ab.

phrases.en: Who's in charge of the music?
phrases.note: Wer = who. Watch out: wo means where, not who. Wer macht ...? = Who's doing ...?
schon wieder = yet again, said with a sigh. das Lied = song, so it's dieses Lied.

phrases.de: Nimm deine Sachen, wir sind da.
phrases.ph: nim DYE-nuh ZA-khen, veer zint dah
phrases.note: Nimm is the command of nehmen (to take); the e changes to i. Sachen = stuff, things — a really useful word.
im is short for in dem. das Auto becomes dem Auto after in when you mean where something is. Present tense covers I'll here.

phrases.en: Are you getting out or not?
phrases.de: Steigst du jetzt aus oder nicht?
phrases.ph: shtykst doo yetst ows OH-der nisht
phrases.note: aussteigen = to get out of a vehicle; the aus splits off to the end. The opposite is einsteigen. jetzt adds impatience.
Steig comes from steigen (to climb). ins = in das, used when you're moving into something.

phrases.en: Hurry up, I'm in the car.
phrases.de: Beeil dich, ich sitze schon im Auto!
phrases.ph: be-ILE dish, ish ZIT-suh shohn im OW-toh
phrases.note: sich beeilen = to hurry. Beeil dich! literally means hurry yourself, and the dich can't be left out.

phrases.de: Hört auf, euch da hinten zu streiten!
phrases.ph: hurt owf, oysh dah HIN-ten tsoo SHTRY-ten
phrases.note: Hört auf is the command for two or more people. sich streiten = to argue, so euch (yourselves) comes with it.
Iss! is the du command of essen (to eat); the e becomes i. Don't confuse it with ist (is).

phrases.en: If you feel sick, tell me.
phrases.de: Wenn dir schlecht wird, sag Bescheid.
phrases.ph: ven deer shlesht virt, zahk be-SHITE
phrases.note: After wenn (if) the verb goes to the end: wenn dir schlecht wird. Bescheid sagen = to let someone know.
aus is always followed by dem/der, so das Fenster becomes aus dem Fenster (out of the window).
rauslassen = to let out, drop off; raus goes to the end. lass is the chatty short form of lasse.
leiser = quieter, from leise (quiet). Mach ... leiser = turn it down; Mach ... lauter = turn it up.
To make a question, just move the verb to the front: Wir sind da becomes Sind wir da? schon = already or yet.
A short, very natural moan: Wie lange noch? is literally How long still? No verb needed.
die Fahrt = the journey or drive, from fahren. Germans use the present tense here, not a will-form.
German splits where: wo = where (at), wohin = where to. Use wohin whenever there's movement.

phrases.en: Can I sit in the front?
phrases.note: vorne = at the front, hinten = at the back. After Darf ich, the main verb sitzen goes to the end.

phrases.en: Can you turn the music up?
phrases.de: Kannst du die Musik lauter machen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo dee moo-ZEEK LOW-ter MA-khen
phrases.note: lauter machen = make louder, i.e. turn up. die Musik is feminine and always takes a capital M.
Here das means it or that. Germans often use das rather than es when pointing at a thing, like the radio.
aussuchen = to pick. At the end of the question it stays in one piece, but it splits in Ich suche die Musik aus.
irgendwo = somewhere. irgend- means some-: irgendwer (someone), irgendwann (sometime). anhalten = to stop the car.
Klo = loo, casual. Ich muss aufs Klo has no go verb — after müssen, Germans often leave gehen out.
Germans have hunger: Ich habe Hunger. Hunger is a noun here, which is why it has a capital H.
Same pattern as Hunger — you have thirst: Ich habe Durst. der Durst is a noun, so capital D.
müde = tired, and it never changes after bin. For extra drama: Ich bin todmüde (dead tired).
Mir ist kalt = literally to me it is cold. Avoid Ich bin kalt — that means you're a cold, unfriendly person.
Always say Mir ist heiß. Ich bin heiß means I'm hot in the attractive sense — very embarrassing in front of Mum!

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating on?
phrases.note: anmachen = to switch on, ausmachen = to switch off. die Heizung = the heating, from heizen (to heat).

phrases.en: Can you turn the air conditioning on?
phrases.note: Klimaanlage = Klima (climate) + Anlage (system). die Anlage decides the gender, so it's die Klimaanlage.
aufmachen = to open, zumachen = to close. They're the chatty versions of öffnen and schließen.

phrases.de: Können wir jetzt nach Hause fahren?
phrases.ph: KUR-nen veer yetst nahkh HOW-zuh FAH-ren
phrases.note: nach Hause = (going) home; zu Hause = at home. Easy to mix up, so link nach with movement.
Mir ist schlecht = I feel sick, word for word to me is bad. Ich bin schlecht would mean I'm bad (at something).
aufladen = to charge a battery. A useful partner phrase: Mein Akku ist leer = my battery's dead.

phrases.en: Can I put my headphones in?
phrases.note: Kopfhörer = headphones, literally head-listeners. Singular and plural look the same: der Kopfhörer, die Kopfhörer.
treten = to kick, and it changes with er: er tritt. For a sister, just swap in Sie tritt ....
der Verkehr = traffic. Its famous partner is der Stau (traffic jam): Wir stehen im Stau = We're stuck in traffic.
wo = where. It looks like who, but who is wer — a classic trap for English speakers.

phrases.en: Can you pass me my bag?
phrases.de: Kannst du mir meine Tasche geben?
phrases.ph: kanst doo meer MY-nuh TA-shuh GAY-ben
phrases.note: mir = to me, so it's literally give to me my bag. die Tasche = bag; a school backpack is der Rucksack.
mitkommen = to come along. The mit splits off and lands at the end: Kommt Monty mit?
aufpassen = to watch out. Here auf appears twice: once as part of the verb at the end, once meaning on. Straße has ß.
Word for word: the sun shines. Germans describe sunny weather like this more than with sonnig. scheinen = to shine.
eiskalt = ice-cold. Adding eis- makes kalt much stronger. Es ist saukalt is a cheekier version.
mitnehmen = to take with you; the mit jumps to the end. der Regenschirm = Regen (rain) + Schirm (shade).
Es ist ... works with lots of weather words: windig (windy), sonnig (sunny), neblig (foggy), bewölkt (cloudy).
sich eincremen = to put cream on yourself. In a command it splits: Creme dich ... ein!
Germans often use the present for the future when a time word is there. Später comes first, so the verb regnet is second.
sich anziehen = to get dressed. Zieh dich warm an is literally dress yourself warm, with the an at the end.
richtig here means really, not just correct. Heute comes first, so ist jumps in front of es (verb second).
glatt = slippery or icy when talking about roads and pavements. It also means smooth. draußen = outside.
mal softens a command a bit, like just: Schau mal! = Have a look! schneien = to snow.
das Gewitter = thunderstorm (thunder and lightning). der Sturm is a storm with strong wind.

phrases.en: Bring the washing in, it's raining.
phrases.de: Hol die Wäsche rein, es regnet!
phrases.ph: hohl dee VE-shuh rine, es RAYK-net
phrases.note: die Wäsche = the washing. reinholen = to bring in; in a command it splits into Hol ... rein!
Germans say die Jacke for most everyday coats. der Mantel is a long, smarter coat.
anziehen = to put on clothes; the an goes last in a command. The opposite is ausziehen (to take off).

phrases.en: You're not going out like that, it's freezing.
phrases.de: So gehst du nicht raus, es ist eiskalt!
phrases.ph: zoh gayst doo nisht rows, es ist ICE-kalt
phrases.note: So = like that. rausgehen = to go outside, and raus sits at the end. A classic parent line.
nass = wet, but before die Schuhe it gets an ending: deine nassen Schuhe. ausziehen splits, so aus goes last.

phrases.en: Shut the door, you're letting the cold in.
phrases.de: Mach die Tür zu, du lässt die Kälte rein!
phrases.ph: makh dee tewr tsoo, doo lest dee KEL-tuh rine
phrases.note: zumachen = to shut. reinlassen = to let in; with du it's lässt, with an ä. die Kälte = the cold.

phrases.en: It's only a bit of rain.
phrases.de: Das ist doch nur ein bisschen Regen.
phrases.ph: das ist dokh noor ine BIS-shen RAY-gen
phrases.note: doch adds a come-on-now feel. ein bisschen = a little bit, and it's written with a small b.
To command one person, take du trinkst and drop du and the -st: Trink! Works for most verbs.
sich erkälten = to catch a cold. noch adds a warning: you'll end up doing it. A cold itself is die Erkältung.
Future pattern: werden + verb at the end. Wird es regnen? = Will it rain?
Wie ist ...? = What's ... like? Swap in anything: Wie ist die Schule? Wie ist das Essen?
No do in German questions: just put the verb first. Brauche ich ...? = Do I need ...?
klatschnass = soaking wet. klatsch- sounds like a splash and makes nass (wet) much stronger.
Not a question: starting with the verb here shows surprise, like What heat! die Hitze = the heat.
frieren = to be freezing (for people). Ich friere sounds stronger than Mir ist kalt.

phrases.en: What's the weather going to be like tomorrow?
phrases.note: wird = will be, from werden. morgen with a small m = tomorrow; der Morgen with a capital = the morning.
hier drin = in here. drin is the everyday short form of darin (in it).
Germans say keine Jacke (no coat), never nicht eine Jacke. A firm, slightly stroppy refusal.

phrases.de: Ich schwitze mich hier drin tot!
phrases.ph: ish SHVIT-suh mish heer drin toht
phrases.note: schwitzen = to sweat. Sweating myself to death is a jokey exaggeration, a bit like I'm boiling.
Schuhe is plural, so it's meine and sind. One shoe = der Schuh; the plural adds -e.

phrases.en: Can you turn the heating up?
phrases.de: Kannst du die Heizung höher drehen?
phrases.ph: kanst doo dee HYE-tsung HUR-er DRAY-en
phrases.note: höher = higher, and drehen = to turn, like turning the dial. Aufdrehen also works.
hassen = to hate. When talking about things in general German drops the the: Ich hasse Regen, Ich hasse Montage.

phrases.en: Can we go to the beach?
phrases.de: Können wir an den Strand fahren?
phrases.ph: KUR-nen veer an dayn shtrant FAH-ren
phrases.note: an den Strand = to the beach (moving there); am Strand = at the beach. der Strand changes to den when you go there.
Weather verbs use es for it: es schneit, es regnet, es hagelt (it's hailing). One word does the whole job.
Just add nicht after ist: Mir ist nicht kalt. Usually said right before refusing a coat.

phrases.en: Can you put the air con on?
phrases.note: die Klima is the everyday short form of die Klimaanlage, just like air con. On its own, Klima also means climate.
Boah is a very German groan (you'll also hear Och nee). schon wieder = yet again.

phrases.de: Jetzt sind meine Haare total durcheinander.
phrases.ph: yetst zint MY-nuh HAH-ruh to-TAHL dursh-ine-AN-der
phrases.note: Germans usually talk about hair as plural: die Haare, so meine Haare sind. durcheinander = messed up.

phrases.en: Can you give me a lift? It's pouring.
phrases.de: Kannst du mich fahren? Es schüttet.
phrases.ph: kanst doo mish FAH-ren es SHEW-tet
phrases.note: Es schüttet = it's pouring, from schütten (to pour). Es regnet in Strömen (in streams) means the same.

phrases.en: What do you want to do this weekend?
phrases.de: Was willst du am Wochenende machen?
phrases.ph: vas vilst doo am VO-khen-en-duh MA-khen
phrases.note: am Wochenende = at the weekend. With willst, the second verb machen goes right to the end.
Wollen wir ...? = Shall we ...? — the German way to suggest doing something. was is short for etwas (something).
Lass uns ... = Let's ... . spazieren gehen = to go for a walk; both verbs sit together at the end.

phrases.en: Shall we watch a film tonight?
phrases.de: Wollen wir heute Abend einen Film schauen?
phrases.ph: VO-len veer HOY-tuh AH-bent EYE-nen film SHOW-en
phrases.note: heute Abend = this evening, tonight. der Film becomes einen Film because it's the thing being watched.
bestellen = to order. Heute Abend comes first, so the verb comes next and wir moves after it.

phrases.en: We're going to Grandma's on Sunday.
phrases.de: Am Sonntag fahren wir zu Oma.
phrases.ph: am ZON-tahk FAH-ren veer tsoo OH-ma
phrases.note: zu Oma = to Grandma's — no word for house needed. Days take am: am Sonntag = on Sunday.

phrases.en: Do you want to come with us?
phrases.note: mitkommen = to come along. It already means with us, so there's no need to add mit uns.
die Eile = hurry, rush. On its own, Keine Eile! = No rush! — handy anywhere.
gewinnen = to win. gerade = right now, which gives the -ing meaning. Another way: Wer liegt vorne?
dran sein = to be someone's turn. Ich bin dran! = My turn! Useful in any game.
weggehen = to go out, leave the house; weg means away. ausgehen is more for a night out.
Parents often shorten this to Schuhe an! — just the thing plus the an from anziehen.
Familienzeit = Familie + n + Zeit. German often adds a linking letter when gluing words; die Zeit sets the gender.
besuchen = to visit people. No the or my needed before Oma, just like Grandma in English.

phrases.en: Turn that off and come outside.
phrases.de: Mach das aus und komm raus!
phrases.ph: makh das ows unt kom rows
phrases.note: ausmachen = to turn off; rauskommen = to come outside. Both split, so aus and raus end up last.

phrases.en: You're coming whether you like it or not.
phrases.de: Du kommst mit, ob du willst oder nicht.
phrases.ph: doo komst mit, op doo vilst OH-der nisht
phrases.note: ob = whether. After ob the verb goes to the end: ob du willst. Firm parent tone — no arguing.

phrases.en: Some fresh air will do you good.
phrases.note: ... tut dir gut = ... does you good. die Luft = air, so the adjective becomes frische.

phrases.en: You can't spend all day in bed.
phrases.de: Du kannst nicht den ganzen Tag im Bett liegen.
phrases.ph: doo kanst nisht dayn GAN-tsen tahk im bet LEE-gen
phrases.note: den ganzen Tag = all day. No word for 'for' or 'during' is needed; the time phrase just sits in the sentence as it is.

phrases.de: Es ist schon fast zwölf Uhr!
phrases.ph: es ist shohn fast tsvurlf oor
phrases.note: fast = nearly, not 'fast' (that's schnell). schon (already) adds the 'can you believe it' tone.

phrases.de: Hör auf zu meckern, das wird lustig.
phrases.ph: hur owf tsoo ME-kern, das virt LUS-tish
phrases.note: meckern = to moan or grumble. Hör auf zu ... = Stop ...ing, a handy pattern: Hör auf zu jammern!
Kopf hoch! literally means 'head up!' It's the standard way to tell someone to cheer up.

phrases.de: Dir ist langweilig? Dann räum dein Zimmer auf.
phrases.ph: deer ist LANG-vy-lish dan roym dine TSI-mer owf
phrases.note: aufräumen (to tidy up) splits in a command: räum ... auf. Dann (then) goes at the front in German, not the end.
gucken is the everyday word for 'watch' at home. The formal-sounding version is anschauen or ansehen.
der Film becomes einen Film here because it's the thing being watched. Masculine words change der/ein to den/einen in that role.
zu Oma = to Grandma's. Families usually drop the article: Oma and Opa are used like names.
Sollen wir ...? = Shall we ...? Swap in any activity: Sollen wir spazieren gehen?

phrases.en: I don't want to watch that.
phrases.note: Starting with Das puts stress on 'that'. The verb will still comes second, and gucken goes to the end.
aussuchen = to pick or choose. Darf ich ...? asks permission, a bit politer than Kann ich ...?

phrases.en: Can we go to the cinema?
phrases.note: ins = in das. das Kino (cinema) is neuter, so 'to the cinema' is ins Kino.
schummeln is the playful word for cheating at games. betrügen is much stronger, more like fraud or cheating on a partner.

phrases.en: What are we doing this weekend?
phrases.note: German uses the present tense for future plans: Was machen wir ...? = What are we doing ...? das Wochenende = the weekend.
Say Mir ist langweilig (literally 'to me it is boring'). Ich bin langweilig means 'I am boring' — a classic mistake!
Es gibt = there is / there are. It's one of the most useful chunks in German: Es gibt Pizza!
ausschlafen = to sleep in, to have a lie-in. One verb does the job of the whole English phrase.
im = in dem. das Bett (bed) is neuter, so 'in bed' becomes im Bett. bleiben = to stay.
mitkommen = to come along. mit (with) is a common add-on: mitgehen, mitnehmen, mitmachen.
was Lustiges = something fun. After was/etwas the adjective gets a capital and an -es ending: was Leckeres, was Neues.

phrases.en: I don't want to go for a walk.
phrases.note: spazieren gehen = to go for a walk. Two verbs together, and both sit at the end after will.
vorhaben = to have planned. It splits: Ich hab was vor. Hab is the chatty short form of habe.

phrases.de: Darf ich mich mit meinen Freundinnen treffen?
phrases.ph: darf ish mish mit MY-nen FROYN-di-nen TRE-fen
phrases.note: Freundinnen = (female) friends. For boys or a mixed group it's Freunden. sich treffen = to meet up.
Spazierengehen is the verb turned into a noun, so it's written as one word with a capital S.

phrases.en: It's the weekend, leave me alone.
phrases.de: Es ist Wochenende, lasst mich in Ruhe.
phrases.ph: es ist VO-khen-en-duh, last mish in ROO-uh
phrases.note: lasst is the ihr form, for talking to several people at once. To one person it's Lass mich in Ruhe! In Ruhe = in peace.
Germans say Essen bestellen (order food) for a takeaway. bestellen = to order, and it looks nothing like the English.
zu Hause = at home, nach Hause = (going) home. Mixing these up is a very common GCSE slip.
Literally 'all the best for your birthday'. der Geburtstag = birthday, from Geburt (birth) + Tag (day).

phrases.en: What do you want for your birthday?
phrases.de: Was wünschst du dir zum Geburtstag?
phrases.ph: vas vewnshst doo deer tsum ge-BOORTS-tahk
phrases.note: sich etwas wünschen = to wish for something. It's the normal way to ask about presents. zum = zu dem.
Wünsch dir was literally means 'wish yourself something'. The dir (yourself) is needed with this verb.
auspusten = to blow out. In a command the aus splits off and goes to the end. die Kerze = candle.
Weihnachten (Christmas) is usually treated as plural here, which is why it's Frohe with an -e.
das Jahr is neuter, so the endings are -es: frohes neues. On New Year's Eve Germans also say Guten Rutsch!
Germans 'make' a party: eine Party machen. You'll also hear feiern, which means to celebrate.

phrases.en: Who do you want to invite?
phrases.note: Wen = who, when the person is the one being invited. wer is for the one doing the action. einladen = to invite.
unterschreiben = to sign. Its past form unterschrieben has no ge- because unter- doesn't split off here.
auspacken = to unwrap. Presents are 'packed out' in German. das Geschenk = present, plural Geschenke.

phrases.en: I can't believe you're fifteen already!
phrases.de: Ich kann nicht glauben, dass du schon fünfzehn bist!
phrases.ph: ish kan nisht GLOW-ben, das doo shohn FEWNF-tsayn bist
phrases.note: After dass (that) the verb goes to the end: dass du schon fünfzehn bist.
Lasst uns ... = Let's ... The action verb goes to the end. Most German families really do sing it in English!
Parents say Wie sagt man? (literally 'how does one say?') to prompt a danke. man = one/people in general.
Sag = say, the command form of sagen. The Danke is capitalised here because it's used like a noun: 'a thank-you'.
noch nicht = not yet. Learn it as one chunk; it goes before the part of the verb that splits off (aus).

phrases.en: Don't invite too many people, OK?
phrases.de: Lad nicht zu viele Leute ein, okay?
phrases.ph: laht nisht tsoo FEE-luh LOY-tuh ine, oh-KAY
phrases.note: einladen splits in a command: Lad ... ein. die Leute = people, and it's always plural.

phrases.de: Die Party ist um elf zu Ende.
phrases.ph: dee PAR-tee ist um elf tsoo EN-duh
phrases.note: zu Ende sein = to be over. um elf = at eleven. Use um for clock times.

phrases.en: Who's going to clear all this up?
phrases.note: Wer = who, when the person does the action. German uses the plain present here (Wer räumt ... auf?) instead of 'going to'.

phrases.en: Go and get changed, the guests are coming.
phrases.de: Zieh dich um, die Gäste kommen gleich.
phrases.ph: tsee dish um, dee GES-tuh KO-men glyesh
phrases.note: sich umziehen = to get changed. It splits: Zieh dich um. der Gast (guest) has an umlaut in the plural: Gäste.

phrases.en: Don't eat all the crisps before they get here.
phrases.de: Iss nicht alle Chips auf, bevor sie da sind.
phrases.ph: is nisht A-luh tships owf, be-FOR zee dah zint
phrases.note: Chips means crisps in German, not chips (those are Pommes). After bevor the verb goes to the end: bevor sie da sind.
Darf ich ...? = Am I allowed to ...? It's the go-to way to ask a parent for permission.
aufmachen = to open, the everyday version of öffnen. With darf ich the whole verb stays together at the end.

phrases.en: I'd like new trainers for my birthday.
phrases.de: Ich wünsch mir neue Turnschuhe zum Geburtstag.
phrases.ph: ish vewnsh meer NOY-uh TURN-shoo-uh tsum ge-BOORTS-tahk
phrases.note: Turnschuhe = trainers, literally 'gym shoes'. Sneaker is also common with teens.

phrases.en: When are we putting the tree up?
phrases.de: Wann stellen wir den Baum auf?
phrases.ph: van SHTE-len veer dayn bowm owf
phrases.note: aufstellen = to put up. It splits: stellen ... auf. Many German families only put the tree up on 24 December.

phrases.de: Wie viele Tage sind es noch bis Weihnachten?
phrases.ph: vee FEE-luh TAH-guh zint es nokh bis VY-nakh-ten
phrases.note: Wie viele ...? = How many ...? Written as two words. noch adds the sense of 'still to go'.
Gibt es ...? = Is there ...? der Kuchen = cake. Birthday cake is often Torte, which is a fancier layered cake.
Danke für ... = Thanks for ... German says 'the presents' (die Geschenke) here, where English says 'my'.
schenken = to give as a present. habt is the ihr form, since the question goes to both parents.
Don't say Ich liebe es for a present — it sounds over the top. Ich finde es toll (I find it great) is what Germans say.

phrases.en: It's not what I asked for.
phrases.de: Das hab ich mir nicht gewünscht.
phrases.ph: das hahp ish meer nisht ge-VEWNSHT
phrases.note: Literally 'I didn't wish for that'. Blunt and a bit ungrateful — fine as a moan at home, rude in front of Grandma.
einladen = to invite. After darf ich it stays in one piece at the end; in a command it splits: Lad sie ein!
Geburtstagsparty = birthday party, glued into one word. The extra s in the middle just joins the two parts.
dekorieren = to decorate, easy to spot. Many verbs borrowed into German end in -ieren: telefonieren, reparieren.
sich freuen = to be happy or excited. Don't use exzitiert — it isn't a word. Ich bin so aufgeregt also works but can mean nervous.
kaum = hardly. Literally 'I can hardly wait for it'. erwarten = to wait for, to expect.
Germans say 'I have birthday': Ich habe Geburtstag. No 'my' and no article needed.
singt is the ihr form, so it's aimed at the whole family. To one person: Bitte sing nicht.
peinlich = embarrassing, a favourite teen word. Ihr seid is for several people; to one parent it's Du bist so peinlich.

phrases.de: Dürfen meine Freundinnen bei uns übernachten?
phrases.ph: DEWR-fen MY-nuh FROYN-di-nen by uns ew-ber-NAKH-ten
phrases.note: Freundinnen = (female) friends; for boys or a mixed group say Freunde. übernachten = to stay the night.

phrases.en: Can you stay upstairs during the party?
phrases.de: Könnt ihr während der Party oben bleiben?
phrases.ph: kurnt eer VAY-rent dayr PAR-tee OH-ben BLY-ben
phrases.note: während = during. It changes die Party to der Party. oben = upstairs, unten = downstairs.
müde = tired. Questions just flip the verb to the front: Du bist müde → Bist du müde?

phrases.en: What time are you going to bed?
phrases.note: ins Bett gehen = to go to bed. ins (in das) shows movement into the bed; im Bett is being in it.

phrases.en: You need to go to bed.
phrases.note: With müssen, Germans often drop the gehen: Du musst ins Bett. The going is understood.
werden = to become or get. Es wird spät = it's getting late. Es wird kalt = it's getting cold.
morgen = tomorrow, but der Morgen = the morning. Morgen früh = tomorrow morning.

phrases.en: Go and get ready for bed.
phrases.note: sich fertig machen = to get ready. bettfertig (bed-ready) is the family version for getting ready for bed.
Zähne putzen = to brush teeth. Geh + another verb at the end = go and do it. No 'and' needed.

phrases.de: Hast du dir die Zähne geputzt?
phrases.ph: hast doo deer dee TSAY-nuh ge-PUTST
phrases.note: Germans say 'brushed yourself the teeth' (dir die Zähne), not 'your teeth'. Same with hair: dir die Haare.
weglegen = to put away. It splits: Leg ... weg. das Handy is the German word for mobile phone.
aufladen = to charge. It splits in a command: Lade ... auf. The same verb is used for topping up credit.
ausmachen = to switch off, and anmachen = to switch on. Both split: Mach das Licht aus / an.
aufbleiben = to stay up. It splits: Bleib ... auf. lange = for a long time; spät (late) is also possible.
noch = still, wach = awake. Handy combo: noch da (still here), noch nicht (not yet).
Warum = why. After a question word the verb comes next: Warum bist du ...?
Schlaf is the command form of schlafen (to sleep). jetzt (now) makes it firmer, as parents do.
die Nacht is feminine, so it's Gute with an -e. Compare Guten Morgen and Guten Tag.
Schlaf gut is the one-to-one version. To several people: Schlaft gut.
Bis ... = See you ... Works with any time: bis später, bis gleich, bis morgen.

phrases.en: Did you have a good day?
phrases.note: hattest = had. schön is often used where English says 'good' or 'nice' about days and holidays.
anziehen = to put on (clothes). It splits: Zieh ... an. der Schlafanzug = pyjamas, but it's singular in German.
Ab ins Bett! is what every German parent says: literally 'off into bed!' No verb needed.

phrases.de: Hast du dir den Wecker gestellt?
phrases.ph: hast doo deer dayn VE-ker ge-SHTELT
phrases.note: der Wecker = alarm clock, from wecken (to wake). Germans still say Wecker when the alarm is on their phone.
lassen = to leave (something somewhere). unten = downstairs. Lass is the command form.

phrases.de: Noch zehn Minuten, dann ist Licht aus.
phrases.ph: nokh tsayn mi-NOO-ten, dan ist lisht ows
phrases.note: Noch zehn Minuten = ten more minutes. dann (then) sends the verb ist straight after it.

phrases.de: Hast du alles für morgen fertig?
phrases.ph: hast doo A-les fewr MOR-gen FER-tish
phrases.note: fertig = ready or finished. Germans more often ask 'have you got everything ready?' than 'is everything ready?'

phrases.en: Do you want a hot chocolate?
phrases.note: der Kakao = hot chocolate. Heiße Schokolade exists but Kakao is the everyday word at home.

phrases.en: Keep the noise down, people are sleeping.
phrases.de: Sei leise, die anderen schlafen schon.
phrases.ph: zye LYE-zuh, dee AN-de-ren SHLAH-fen shohn
phrases.note: Sei leise = be quiet. Sei is the command form of sein (to be). die anderen = the others.
Germans say 'dream something nice'. Träum comes from träumen, and Schönes has a capital after was.
Hab dich lieb is the family way to say love you. Ich liebe dich is mostly for romantic love.
müde = tired. The ü is a proper sound: say 'ee' with rounded lips.
Present tense works for 'I'm going to'. Geh is the chatty short form of gehe.
nicht (not) goes before the describing word: nicht müde, nicht fertig, nicht hungrig.

phrases.en: I'm not going to bed yet.
phrases.de: Ich geh noch nicht ins Bett.
phrases.ph: ish gay nokh nisht ins bet
phrases.note: noch nicht = not yet. Keep the two words together as a chunk before ins Bett.

phrases.de: So spät ist es doch gar nicht.
phrases.ph: zoh shpayt ist es dokh gahr nisht
phrases.note: doch adds an arguing 'come on' tone, and gar nicht = not at all. Classic backchat.
Nur noch = just ... more. Swap in anything: Nur noch eine Folge! (just one more episode).

phrases.de: Ich mach das nur noch fertig.
phrases.ph: ish makh das noor nokh FER-tish
phrases.note: fertig machen = to finish off. nur noch here means 'just'. No -ing form in German; the present does the job.
duschen = to shower, one verb. erst = first. Ich geh duschen = I'm going for a shower.
Wo = where (not 'who' — that's wer). das Ladekabel = charging cable, what Germans usually call a charger.
der Schlafanzug is masculine, so mein becomes meinen as the thing being seen. gesehen = seen.

phrases.en: Can you turn the light off?
phrases.note: Kannst du ...? = Can you ...? After kannst du the verb goes to the end in one piece: ausmachen.
zumachen = to shut; aufmachen = to open. Mach die Tür zu is blunt — add bitte to soften it.
offen = open (describing word). die Tür is feminine, so it's die Tür.
Just Nacht! is the casual teen version of Gute Nacht. Fine with family, a bit short with anyone else.
Bis morgen = until tomorrow. Bis is the key word in lots of goodbyes: Bis dann! Bis bald!
kann (can) sends the second verb to the end: Ich kann nicht schlafen.
der Albtraum = nightmare; der Traum = dream. einen shows it's the thing you had.

phrases.en: Can you wake me up at seven?
phrases.de: Kannst du mich um sieben wecken?
phrases.ph: kanst doo mish um ZEE-ben VE-ken
phrases.note: wecken = to wake someone up. mich (me) comes early, and wecken goes to the end.

phrases.de: Ich hab mir den Wecker gestellt.
phrases.ph: ish hahp meer dayn VE-ker ge-SHTELT
phrases.note: den Wecker stellen = to set the alarm. stellen normally means to put or stand something.
Schlaf schön is a warm alternative to Schlaf gut. Both are fine to say to a parent.

phrases.en: Can I read for a bit?
phrases.de: Darf ich noch ein bisschen lesen?
phrases.ph: darf ish nokh ine BIS-shen LAY-zen
phrases.note: ein bisschen = a bit. With noch it means 'a bit longer'. lesen = to read.

phrases.en: Can Monty sleep in my room?
phrases.de: Darf Monty in meinem Zimmer schlafen?
phrases.ph: darf MON-tee in MY-nem TSI-mer SHLAH-fen
phrases.note: das Zimmer is neuter, and after in (where something is) mein becomes meinem.

phrases.en: I'm cold, can I have another blanket?
phrases.de: Mir ist kalt, kann ich noch eine Decke haben?
phrases.ph: meer ist kalt, kan ish nokh EYE-nuh DE-kuh HAH-ben
phrases.note: Say Mir ist kalt for 'I'm cold'. Ich bin kalt means you're a cold-hearted person! noch eine = another.

phrases.en: What time do I have to get up?
phrases.note: aufstehen = to get up. With muss it stays whole at the end; alone it splits: Ich stehe um sieben auf.
